# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region, Spanish Colonial Period (Pre-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Established:** Arkansas Post, the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley, was founded by the French in 1686 on the Arkansas River near its confluence with the Mississippi River
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post — the only permanent European settlement in the region throughout this period
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana: French colonial administration 1686-1763; Spanish colonial administration 1763-1800 (Treaty of Paris 1763); secretly ceded back to France in 1800 (Treaty of San Ildefonso); transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Arkansas Territory organized 1819; statehood 1836
- **Population during period:** FamilySearch tools returned no population figures for pre-1800 Arkansas; European settlement was extremely sparse and concentrated almost entirely at Arkansas Post and its immediate vicinity
- **Economy:** Fur trade, river commerce, and a Spanish colonial military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish settlers, mixed-race traders (metis), Native Americans (principally the Quapaw and Osage), and enslaved Africans and African Americans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only formally organized denomination in this colonial region)
- **Key historical events:** Cession to Spain under the 1763 Treaty of Paris; Battle of Arkansas Post (1783) against British forces; secret retrocession to France in 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- The pre-1800 Arkansas region had no formal county or territorial subdivision; the entire area was governed as part of the Province of Louisiana administered from New Orleans
- French control: 1686-1763; Spanish control: 1763-1800; no U.S. county government or territorial organization existed during this period
- Records from before 1800 therefore follow the Spanish (and earlier French) colonial administrative chain — New Orleans and ultimately Seville — rather than any U.S. state or county structure
- The transition from French to Spanish administration in 1763 split the record series: French-era records are in French; post-1763 records are in Spanish
- After the Louisiana Purchase (1803) and the organization of Arkansas Territory (1819), American county structures were established, but these postdate the target period

## Available record types

Note: No U.S. civil registration infrastructure existed in this region before 1800. The record-keeping authority was the Spanish (and earlier French) colonial military and ecclesiastical administration at Arkansas Post. All record types listed below were generated at the post level, not at any county or state level.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this region during the pre-1800 colonial period; the FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Arkansas-specific vital records page during this survey
- **What exists:** No state or territorial civil registration for this period; vital events were recorded only through the Catholic Church
- **Where held:** See Church Records section below
- **Gaps:** Complete absence of civil registration for 1686-1800
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers are the only surviving vital record equivalents

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic; French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; the registers document European settlers, mixed-race persons, and Native Americans
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch has 1 digitized volume (DGS 008814402): Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800, 64 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), **in Spanish**
  - Originals and transcriptions also held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)
  - French-era registers (pre-1763) may survive and are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission
- **Language:** French for pre-1763 records; Spanish for 1763-1800 records

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No U.S. census was taken in this region before 1800; the first applicable federal census was 1820 (after Arkansas Territory was organized)
- **Colonial census equivalents (padrones):** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) were conducted during the 1763-1800 period at Arkansas Post and are held at the Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, and the Archivo General de Indias, Seville (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Access:** Physical only — not digitized on FamilySearch; Library of Congress holds microfilm of some Spanish colonial records

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish civil and military administrative records from the Arkansas Post garrison; no organized county court existed during this period
- **Date range:** 1763-1800 (Spanish); earlier French records may exist
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish colonial land concessions; the U.S. rectangular survey system did not apply during this period
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial governor in New Orleans, granting concessions in the Province of Louisiana
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions (grants/patents) confirmed as existing for this period (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); French grants pre-1763
- **Date range:** French grants 1686-1763; Spanish concessions 1763-1800
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm — physical only, not digitized on FamilySearch

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish colonial garrison activity at Arkansas Post (1763-1800); Battle of Arkansas Post (1783) against British forces
- **Record types:** Civil and military post records confirmed as existing (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records); troop rosters, garrison correspondence, administrative papers
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Library of Congress microfilm

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** No specific named cemeteries for this period were returned by tool results; a Catholic burial ground associated with Arkansas Post would have existed
- **Online coverage:** FamilySearch tools returned no cemetery collections for this place and period
- **Physical records:** Arkansas History Commission may hold documentation; contact the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock for burial register information

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers documented for Arkansas Post during the colonial period; none returned by tools
- **Where held:** N/A for pre-1800

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary entry point for the Province of Louisiana; the Mississippi River was the principal travel corridor
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial administrative records and ship manifests through New Orleans; records for this period are sparse and largely held in Spanish archives
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Louisiana State Archives (records entering through New Orleans)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** No documented tax records returned by tools for pre-1800 Arkansas specifically; Spanish padrones may serve a similar enumeration function
- **Date range:** N/A as documented by tools
- **Substitute value:** Spanish padrones (colonial censuses) served as population registers during this period

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial administrative correspondence:** Civil and military correspondence, orders, and reports for the Arkansas Post garrison (1763-1800) are held at the Archivo General de Indias and the Arkansas History Commission

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800 (DGS 008814402), 64 images, browse-only, in Spanish | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | General U.S. records; see physical holdings below | Free to search |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matched this place and period; the result set is complete (1 of 1 returned). FamilySearch's 3 indexed collections for Arkansas all begin in 1819 or later and do not cover the colonial period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial censuses (padrones), land concessions, civil and military records, sacramental register transcriptions (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) | In-person or written inquiry |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records for the Province of Louisiana, including Arkansas Post records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) | In-person; some records microfilmed by the Library of Congress |
| Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. | Microfilm of Spanish colonial records for the Province of Louisiana (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from French and Spanish colonial periods (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) | Contact the Diocese directly |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) from Arkansas Post — physical only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish land concessions — physical only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish civil and military administrative correspondence — physical only
- French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763) — physical only at the Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission
- The one digitized FamilySearch volume (DGS 008814402) is online but browse-only and in Spanish; no name index exists

## Known record losses
- No specific record destructions were returned by tool results for this period; however, given the remote nature of Arkansas Post and the administrative transitions from French to Spanish to American authority, record survival is uneven and gaps should be expected
- Records not transferred to successor repositories during the 1800-1803 transition from Spanish to French to American authority may have been lost

## Research tips
- Arkansas Post was the only significant European settlement in pre-1800 Arkansas; if your ancestor lived in this region before 1800, they almost certainly appear (if at all) in Arkansas Post records — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- The FamilySearch digitized volume (DGS 008814402) must be browsed image by image with no name search and is in Spanish; plan to review all 64 images
- Search the Archivo General de Indias online portal (portal.archivodeindias.es) for inventories of Louisiana colonial records, and contact the Library of Congress for microfilm access to the same — per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- Colonial Louisiana records (especially those from New Orleans) are essential complements; Arkansas Post was administratively subordinate to New Orleans, and many records about Post inhabitants may appear in Louisiana provincial collections rather than Arkansas-specific ones
- All four FamilySearch Wiki research guide pages for Arkansas (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy directly for Arkansas-specific research guidance
- Records are in French (pre-1763) and Spanish (1763-1800); a researcher must read these languages or obtain translations

Here is what the locality guide returned:

---

**Locality Guide: Ohio circa 1790 — Pre-Statehood (Northwest Territory)**

In 1790, present-day Ohio did not yet exist as a state — it was the **Northwest Territory**, organized under federal authority in 1787. Only two counties had been carved out within what became Ohio at that time:

- **Washington County** (1788, centered at Marietta)
- **Hamilton County** (1790, centered at Cincinnati)

Everything else was unorganized land with no local record-making infrastructure at all.

---

### Boundary Changes & Jurisdictional History

Ohio did not become a state until **March 1, 1803**, so any event before that date must be searched under **"Northwest Territory"** and the early county names — not under later Ohio county names that didn't exist yet. This is a critical framing point for any pre-statehood research.

---

### What Records Are Available Despite Early Gaps

Because no civil system recorded births or deaths, the most useful records for this period are:

1. **Land Transactions** — Ohio contains three competing land-grant systems, and which archive holds your ancestor's records depends on *which part of Ohio* they settled in:
   - **Virginia Military District** → records at the Virginia State Library
   - **Connecticut Western Reserve** → records at the Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland)
   - **Federal Rectangular-Survey Lands** → land patents free at the [BLM GLO website](https://glorecords.blm.gov)

2. **Church Registers** — Often the only source for births and deaths in this era.

3. **County Marriage Records** — Begin as early as **1789** in Washington and Hamilton counties.

4. **Federal Census** — The **1790 and 1800 federal censuses** are primary sources for identifying households in the pre-statehood period.

---

### Key Research Warning

Any search for pre-1803 events must use **"Northwest Territory"** and the early county names. Later Ohio county boundaries simply did not exist and searching under them will miss records entirely.

---

**Recommended next step:** Use this locality guide to build a targeted research plan focused on land records, church registers, and the 1790/1800 federal censuses for your specific ancestor.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (ca. 1790, pre-statehood period 1787-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was organized July 13, 1787 under the Northwest Ordinance. Washington County (the first Ohio county) was organized in 1788; Hamilton County in 1790. Ohio achieved statehood March 1, 1803 as the first state carved from the territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Washington County seat: Marietta (first permanent American settlement, 1788). Hamilton County seat: Cincinnati (established 1789).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory of the United States (federal, 1787-1803), then Ohio, United States (from 1803)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this period. Settlement was extremely sparse in 1790, confined largely to the Marietta garrison area and frontier posts along the Ohio River.
- **Economy:** Frontier/military settlement, subsistence farming, fur trade, land speculation.
- **Ethnic composition:** New England migrants (Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio), Virginians (Virginia Military District), mixed frontier settlers from Pennsylvania and the mid-Atlantic states; large Native American presence (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami).
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Congregationalist (Connecticut migrants). Earliest organized congregations at Marietta and Cincinnati, ca. 1788-1793.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Indian War 1790-1795 (including the defeat at the Battle of the Wabash, 1791, and Anthony Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers, 1794); Treaty of Greenville 1795 (opened most of Ohio to settlement); Enabling Act 1802; Ohio statehood March 1, 1803.

## Boundary changes

This is the critical research issue for 1790 Ohio. The period involves both a temporal split (territorial versus state records) and a geographic split (three competing land-grant systems).

**Temporal split:**
- Before March 1, 1803: Present-day Ohio was the Northwest Territory. Any court, land, or administrative record created before that date was created under territorial authority. Within the territory, Washington County (from 1788) and Hamilton County (from 1790) held local court and land records for their geographic portions. All other areas of present-day Ohio were unorganized — no county existed, no local record-making infrastructure.
- After March 1, 1803: Ohio counties took over record-keeping. County formation was rapid after statehood.
- **Research consequence:** An event in present-day Ohio in 1790 would be recorded — if at all — either in territorial-level records or in Washington County / Hamilton County records. Searching under later county names will miss territorial-era records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)): boundary changes were frequent; researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.

**Geographic split — three land-grant systems:**
Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)):
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto River and Little Miami River): Reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Metes-and-bounds survey. Virginia issued the warrants; those records are at the Virginia State Library.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Conveyed to Connecticut. Different township grid survey. Records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Federal rectangular survey** (the rest of Ohio): U.S. General Land Office issued patents, now searchable at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Research consequence:** Which archive to search depends entirely on where within Ohio your ancestor settled. These systems do not align with county boundaries.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in 1790. County-level marriage records begin as early as 1789 (FamilySearch collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013'). The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records directly for precise start dates and levels for births and deaths.
- **What exists:** Marriage records at county level from 1789 in Washington and Hamilton counties. No organized civil birth or death registration in 1790 — these events were recorded only in church registers.
- **Where held:** Early county marriage records are at the Ohio History Connection, Columbus, and county courthouses. FamilySearch collection [Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) (1,523,678 records, indexed with images) is the primary online resource.
- **Gaps:** The bulk of 1790 Ohio was unorganized territory with no county infrastructure. Expect major gaps in all record types outside Washington and Hamilton counties.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Congregationalist. Earliest organized frontier congregations at Marietta (1788) and Cincinnati/Hamilton County area (ca. 1790-1793).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event and may be the only surviving record of a birth year. Circuit-rider Methodist records may be scattered across conference archives.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) (678,234 records, indexed) begins in 1787. Denominational archives and the Ohio History Connection hold additional originals.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census covered the Northwest Territory (though Ohio settlement coverage is thin). The 1800 federal census covers Ohio as a territory. Both are indexed and available at Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).
- **State/territorial census:** No separate territorial enumeration of Ohio is known for 1790.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists from 1800 onward partially substitute for intercensal years. Mortality schedules (1850-1885) record deaths in the preceding year — background context only, not applicable to 1790.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal census records are name-indexed online at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate), estate administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories. In the territorial period (1790), territorial courts in Washington County and Hamilton County handled these.
- **Date range:** Washington County territorial court records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- **Where held:** Early court and land records are at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)). The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey run; consult it directly for digitized or microfilmed volumes of Washington County and Hamilton County probate.

### Land records

- **Survey systems:** Three coexist (see Boundary changes above).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia issued Military District warrants (Virginia State Library); the U.S. General Land Office issued federal-survey patents (BLM GLO); Connecticut oversaw the Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society).
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, deeds, surveys, bounty land warrants (Revolutionary War veterans in Virginia Military District), tax records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) (234,567 records, indexed) begins 1787. FamilySearch also holds a digitized volume of Northwest Territory territorial land records 1788-1799 (imageGroupNumber 005112233, 51 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** Virginia State Library (Richmond) for Military District; Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) for Western Reserve; BLM GLO online for federal-survey lands; Ohio History Connection for territorial records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War 1790-1795. Revolutionary War veterans were among the earliest Ohio settlers, particularly in the Virginia Military District.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files; bounty land warrants (for the Virginia Military District); Northwest Indian War service records.
- **Where held:** NARA (National Archives) holds service and pension records. Fold3.com (subscription) provides online access. BLM GLO holds bounty land warrant records for federal-survey lands.

### Cemetery records

- **Earliest cemeteries:** The oldest American cemetery in Ohio is at Marietta (Washington County), established 1788. Military cemeteries from early frontier posts also exist.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover some early Ohio cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the earliest frontier settlements are fragmentary or nonexistent; church burial registers are the primary alternative.

### Newspaper records

- **Earliest Ohio newspaper:** The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* began publication in Cincinnati in 1793 — after 1790. No Ohio newspaper predates 1793.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) and Ohio Memory (ohiomemory.org) hold digitized Ohio newspaper runs. State library microfilm collections.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for 1790 (no newspapers existed). Marriage notices and obituaries become useful from the mid-1790s onward.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Most 1790 settlers arrived overland from the east or by flatboat down the Ohio River from Pittsburgh. Key entry points: Marietta and Cincinnati on the Ohio River, and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions (filed in any court of record pre-1906; territorial and early county courts at Ohio History Connection); no ocean passenger lists are relevant for internal migrants from the eastern states.
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal naturalization records post-1906. Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial and county court records at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Content note:** If an ancestor immigrated from Europe before settling in Ohio, search ocean passenger arrival records at Atlantic ports (Philadelphia, Baltimore, New York) through NARA and Ancestry.com. Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and young children — examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) (345,890 records, indexed) begins at 1800. A digitized volume of Washington County tax records 1799-1803 (imageGroupNumber 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed) is available but is mostly browse-only.
- **Where held:** County auditor / county courthouse; Ohio History Connection for earliest territorial-era records.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are critical substitutes for missing early census records and can confirm an ancestor's presence in a county in a given year.

### Other record types

- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century county histories for Washington and Hamilton counties reprint early territorial records and name early settlers found nowhere else — often the only surviving transcription of records since lost.
- **Survey field notes:** Surveyors who mapped Ohio in the 1780s-1790s noted natural features and sometimes named early occupants. These are at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Territorial legislative and administrative records:** Governor St. Clair's administrative papers and territorial legislature records are at NARA and the Ohio History Connection.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1.5M records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678K records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (235K records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (346K records); 2 digitized volumes for territorial period (browse-only or partially indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 U.S. Federal Census (Northwest Territory / Ohio Territory coverage) | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War and early federal military records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for rectangular-survey Ohio lands | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records including early Ohio pioneer burials | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Ohio newspapers (earliest 1793) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military, naturalization, federal administrative records | In-person / online request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching the 1780-1810 target period; this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The collections_search returned 5 collections for the Ohio scope; 3 (marriages, church, land) begin at or before 1790. No volume_search summary was returned by the tool.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus, OH) | Early territorial court records, Washington and Hamilton County records, survey field notes, county histories | In-person; some by request |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District land warrants and surveys | In-person / mail request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records and surveys | In-person / mail request |
| Washington County Courthouse (Marietta, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1788 | In-person |
| Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1790 | In-person |
| NARA (multiple locations) | Revolutionary War pensions, service records, early federal land office records | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online

- **Territorial court records** (Washington County and Hamilton County, 1788-1803): held physically at the Ohio History Connection; the FamilySearch digitized volume (005112233) of territorial land records 1788-1799 is browse-only.
- **Virginia Military District land warrants** (pre-1803): at the Virginia State Library; not fully digitized or name-indexed.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve land records**: at the Western Reserve Historical Society; not fully digitized.
- **Early frontier church registers** for specific congregations: many are undigitized, held at local churches or denominational archives.
- **Survey field notes** from 1780s-1790s: at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Governor St. Clair's administrative papers**: at NARA and Ohio History Connection.

## Known record losses

- **Records for unorganized territory before 1788:** Before Washington County was organized in 1788, essentially no local civil record-keeping existed in present-day Ohio. Events in 1787 and earlier generated no county-level records.
- **Northwest Indian War disruption (1790-1795):** The war caused significant population displacement and frontier abandonment. Some settlers appearing in 1788-1790 Washington County records may have fled and re-appear only after 1795. Expect gaps in a person's trail during this period.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (ca. 1790, pre-statehood period 1787-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Northwest Territory was organized July 13, 1787 under the Northwest Ordinance. Washington County (the first Ohio county) was organized in 1788; Hamilton County in 1790. Ohio achieved statehood March 1, 1803 as the first state carved from the territory.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Washington County seat: Marietta (first permanent American settlement, 1788). Hamilton County seat: Cincinnati (established 1789).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory of the United States (federal, 1787-1803), then Ohio, United States (from 1803)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this period. Settlement was extremely sparse in 1790, confined largely to the Marietta garrison area and frontier posts along the Ohio River.
- **Economy:** Frontier/military settlement, subsistence farming, fur trade, land speculation.
- **Ethnic composition:** New England migrants (Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio), Virginians (Virginia Military District), mixed frontier settlers from Pennsylvania and the mid-Atlantic states; large Native American presence (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami).
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Congregationalist (Connecticut migrants). Earliest organized congregations at Marietta and Cincinnati, ca. 1788-1793.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Indian War 1790-1795 (including the defeat at the Battle of the Wabash, 1791, and Anthony Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers, 1794); Treaty of Greenville 1795 (opened most of Ohio to settlement); Enabling Act 1802; Ohio statehood March 1, 1803.

## Boundary changes

This is the critical research issue for 1790 Ohio. The period involves both a temporal split (territorial versus state records) and a geographic split (three competing land-grant systems).

**Temporal split:**
- Before March 1, 1803: Present-day Ohio was the Northwest Territory. Any court, land, or administrative record created before that date was created under territorial authority. Within the territory, Washington County (from 1788) and Hamilton County (from 1790) held local court and land records for their geographic portions. All other areas of present-day Ohio were unorganized — no county existed, no local record-making infrastructure.
- After March 1, 1803: Ohio counties took over record-keeping. County formation was rapid after statehood.
- **Research consequence:** An event in present-day Ohio in 1790 would be recorded — if at all — either in territorial-level records or in Washington County / Hamilton County records. Searching under later county names will miss territorial-era records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)): boundary changes were frequent; researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.

**Geographic split — three land-grant systems:**
Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)):
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto River and Little Miami River): Reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Metes-and-bounds survey. Virginia issued the warrants; those records are at the Virginia State Library.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Conveyed to Connecticut. Different township grid survey. Records at the Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland.
- **Federal rectangular survey** (the rest of Ohio): U.S. General Land Office issued patents, now searchable at BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Research consequence:** Which archive to search depends entirely on where within Ohio your ancestor settled. These systems do not align with county boundaries.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed in 1790. County-level marriage records begin as early as 1789 (FamilySearch collection 'Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013'). The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records directly for precise start dates and levels for births and deaths.
- **What exists:** Marriage records at county level from 1789 in Washington and Hamilton counties. No organized civil birth or death registration in 1790 — these events were recorded only in church registers.
- **Where held:** Early county marriage records are at the Ohio History Connection, Columbus, and county courthouses. FamilySearch collection [Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) (1,523,678 records, indexed with images) is the primary online resource.
- **Gaps:** The bulk of 1790 Ohio was unorganized territory with no county infrastructure. Expect major gaps in all record types outside Washington and Hamilton counties.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker, Congregationalist. Earliest organized frontier congregations at Marietta (1788) and Cincinnati/Hamilton County area (ca. 1790-1793).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event and may be the only surviving record of a birth year. Circuit-rider Methodist records may be scattered across conference archives.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) (678,234 records, indexed) begins in 1787. Denominational archives and the Ohio History Connection hold additional originals.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census covered the Northwest Territory (though Ohio settlement coverage is thin). The 1800 federal census covers Ohio as a territory. Both are indexed and available at Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).
- **State/territorial census:** No separate territorial enumeration of Ohio is known for 1790.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists from 1800 onward partially substitute for intercensal years. Mortality schedules (1850-1885) record deaths in the preceding year — background context only, not applicable to 1790.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal census records are name-indexed online at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills (testate), estate administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories. In the territorial period (1790), territorial courts in Washington County and Hamilton County handled these.
- **Date range:** Washington County territorial court records from 1788; Hamilton County from 1790.
- **Where held:** Early court and land records are at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)). The FamilySearch Catalog was not searched in this survey run; consult it directly for digitized or microfilmed volumes of Washington County and Hamilton County probate.

### Land records

- **Survey systems:** Three coexist (see Boundary changes above).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia issued Military District warrants (Virginia State Library); the U.S. General Land Office issued federal-survey patents (BLM GLO); Connecticut oversaw the Western Reserve (Western Reserve Historical Society).
- **Types:** Land grants, patents, deeds, surveys, bounty land warrants (Revolutionary War veterans in Virginia Military District), tax records.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) (234,567 records, indexed) begins 1787. FamilySearch also holds a digitized volume of Northwest Territory territorial land records 1788-1799 (imageGroupNumber 005112233, 51 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image).
- **Where held:** Virginia State Library (Richmond) for Military District; Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) for Western Reserve; BLM GLO online for federal-survey lands; Ohio History Connection for territorial records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War 1790-1795. Revolutionary War veterans were among the earliest Ohio settlers, particularly in the Virginia Military District.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files; bounty land warrants (for the Virginia Military District); Northwest Indian War service records.
- **Where held:** NARA (National Archives) holds service and pension records. Fold3.com (subscription) provides online access. BLM GLO holds bounty land warrant records for federal-survey lands.

### Cemetery records

- **Earliest cemeteries:** The oldest American cemetery in Ohio is at Marietta (Washington County), established 1788. Military cemeteries from early frontier posts also exist.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves cover some early Ohio cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the earliest frontier settlements are fragmentary or nonexistent; church burial registers are the primary alternative.

### Newspaper records

- **Earliest Ohio newspaper:** The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* began publication in Cincinnati in 1793 — after 1790. No Ohio newspaper predates 1793.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) and Ohio Memory (ohiomemory.org) hold digitized Ohio newspaper runs. State library microfilm collections.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for 1790 (no newspapers existed). Marriage notices and obituaries become useful from the mid-1790s onward.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant routes:** Most 1790 settlers arrived overland from the east or by flatboat down the Ohio River from Pittsburgh. Key entry points: Marietta and Cincinnati on the Ohio River, and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions (filed in any court of record pre-1906; territorial and early county courts at Ohio History Connection); no ocean passenger lists are relevant for internal migrants from the eastern states.
- **Where held:** NARA holds federal naturalization records post-1906. Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial and county court records at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Content note:** If an ancestor immigrated from Europe before settling in Ohio, search ocean passenger arrival records at Atlantic ports (Philadelphia, Baltimore, New York) through NARA and Ancestry.com. Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and young children — examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection [Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) (345,890 records, indexed) begins at 1800. A digitized volume of Washington County tax records 1799-1803 (imageGroupNumber 005112240, 73 images, 12% name-indexed) is available but is mostly browse-only.
- **Where held:** County auditor / county courthouse; Ohio History Connection for earliest territorial-era records.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are critical substitutes for missing early census records and can confirm an ancestor's presence in a county in a given year.

### Other record types

- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century county histories for Washington and Hamilton counties reprint early territorial records and name early settlers found nowhere else — often the only surviving transcription of records since lost.
- **Survey field notes:** Surveyors who mapped Ohio in the 1780s-1790s noted natural features and sometimes named early occupants. These are at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Territorial legislative and administrative records:** Governor St. Clair's administrative papers and territorial legislature records are at NARA and the Ohio History Connection.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1.5M records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678K records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (235K records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (346K records); 2 digitized volumes for territorial period (browse-only or partially indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 U.S. Federal Census (Northwest Territory / Ohio Territory coverage) | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Revolutionary War and early federal military records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for rectangular-survey Ohio lands | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records including early Ohio pioneer burials | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Ohio newspapers (earliest 1793) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military, naturalization, federal administrative records | In-person / online request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching the 1780-1810 target period; this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). The collections_search returned 5 collections for the Ohio scope; 3 (marriages, church, land) begin at or before 1790. No volume_search summary was returned by the tool.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus, OH) | Early territorial court records, Washington and Hamilton County records, survey field notes, county histories | In-person; some by request |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District land warrants and surveys | In-person / mail request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records and surveys | In-person / mail request |
| Washington County Courthouse (Marietta, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1788 | In-person |
| Hamilton County Courthouse (Cincinnati, OH) | County deeds, marriages, probate from 1790 | In-person |
| NARA (multiple locations) | Revolutionary War pensions, service records, early federal land office records | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online

- **Territorial court records** (Washington County and Hamilton County, 1788-1803): held physically at the Ohio History Connection; the FamilySearch digitized volume (005112233) of territorial land records 1788-1799 is browse-only.
- **Virginia Military District land warrants** (pre-1803): at the Virginia State Library; not fully digitized or name-indexed.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve land records**: at the Western Reserve Historical Society; not fully digitized.
- **Early frontier church registers** for specific congregations: many are undigitized, held at local churches or denominational archives.
- **Survey field notes** from 1780s-1790s: at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Governor St. Clair's administrative papers**: at NARA and Ohio History Connection.

## Known record losses

- **Records for unorganized territory before 1788:** Before Washington County was organized in 1788, essentially no local civil record-keeping existed in present-day Ohio. Events in 1787 and earlier generated no county-level records.
- **Northwest Indian War disruption (1790-1795):** The war caused significant population displacement and frontier abandonment. Some settlers appearing in 1788-1790 Washington County records may have fled and re-appear only after 1795. Expect gaps in a person's trail during this period.
- **Inherent sparseness:** Washington County's earliest records (1788-1800) are extremely thin simply because the county held very few people; expect sparse coverage as a structural gap, not just a loss event.

## Research tips

1. **Identify the county of jurisdiction before searching.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Northwest Territory section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)), only Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790) existed in Ohio in 1790, and boundary changes after 1800 were frequent — the county that filed a record may not be the modern county covering that location.
2. **Land records and church records are the strongest primary sources for 1790.** No civil vital registration existed for births and deaths; land transactions and church baptisms/marriages/burials are the backbone of research for this period.
3. **Virginia Military District researchers must go to Virginia.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy, Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)), Virginia issued those land warrants and those records are at the Virginia State Library — not at Ohio archives. Use BLM GLO for federal-survey-area Ohio lands.
4. **Search under 'Northwest Territory' as well as county names** in catalogs and databases — the FamilySearch Catalog and NARA both file pre-1803 territorial records under the territory name.
5. **The 1790 federal census covered the Northwest Territory** — search it for ancestors who may appear there, but expect thin coverage given sparse settlement.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content** during this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy directly before finalizing your research plan.

California during the Gold Rush (1848–1865) is one of the most complex research environments in American genealogy: the state skipped territorial status entirely, was formed out of Mexican territory in 1850, and received roughly 300,000 migrants within a few years. Here's a breakdown of the key records and repositories:

---

## Key Records

### Census Records
- **1852 California State Census** — Available on FamilySearch, ~88% name-indexed. This is especially critical because the 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed and some county returns are entirely missing.

### Vital & Civil Records
- **County-level birth and marriage records** begin in 1850, but civil registration was not uniformly enforced. **Church records, probate files, and tax rolls** often fill the gaps.

### Mining Records
- **Mining claim registers** were filed at the county recorder's office of whichever county the claim was located in. You must identify the specific mining county first — key counties include **El Dorado, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, and Placer**.
- FamilySearch holds browsable but **unindexed** Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco (1849–1855) — these must be examined image by image.

### Immigration & Arrival Records
- **Ship passenger manifests** for San Francisco arrivals are held at the **National Archives facility in San Bruno, California**.
- FamilySearch also holds unindexed Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento (1849–1858).

### Voter Registration
- **California Great Registers** (voter registration, beginning 1866) post-date the Gold Rush window but are invaluable for migrants who stayed — they record physical description, occupation, and birthplace.

---

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | 1852 state census, mining claim registers, port arrivals, probate records |
| **National Archives – San Bruno, CA** | Ship passenger manifests, federal land records |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Largest manuscript collection of Gold Rush-era personal papers and diaries |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscripts, newspapers, state records |
| **County Recorder's Offices** | Mining claims, deeds, marriages, early vital records |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California was admitted to the Union on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. Before 1848 it was Mexican Alta California; from 1848–1850 it was under U.S. military governance.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); Gold Rush counties include El Dorado (Placerville), Nevada (Nevada City), Calaveras (San Andreas), Tuolumne (Sonora), Amador (Jackson), Placer (Auburn).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (federal); formerly Mexico.
- **Population during period:** Approximately 300,000 people arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855) according to Wikipedia. The population was overwhelmingly male and highly transient.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated; merchant trade, shipping, agriculture, and service industries developed rapidly around mining camps.
- **Ethnic composition:** Exceptionally diverse — American migrants from the eastern states, Chileans, Chinese, Mexicans, Australians, and Europeans. Chinese immigrants were present in large numbers from the early 1850s and left records in both U.S. and Chinese sources.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (established through the Mission system and continuing with Irish and Mexican Catholic parishes), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and various other Protestant denominations arrived with the miners.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; California county system established 1850; influx of Chinese immigration from early 1850s onward.

## Boundary changes
- Before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 2, 1848), California was Mexican territory. Records from the Spanish colonial and Mexican periods are held in Mexican civil and church archives and in California mission registers.
- From 1848 to 1850, California was under U.S. military governance — some records from this interregnum survive in military files at NARA.
- California was admitted as a state in 1850 with a county system created at statehood. New counties were carved out as population shifted; the specific county where a mining claim or settlement was located determines where county-level records were filed.
- Boundaries were relatively stable after 1850, though several mining-area counties were subdivided (e.g., Amador County created from El Dorado and Calaveras Counties in 1854).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki California Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey — no California-specific registration start date and level could be confirmed from a returned source URL. Do not assume statewide civil registration existed in the 1850s; many U.S. states did not require it until the early 1900s.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (collection 2017276, approximately 789,456 records) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (collection 1452832, approximately 567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons). These are county-level records, not state-mandated registration.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for originals; FamilySearch online collections for digitized copies.
- **Gaps:** County compliance and completeness varied widely in the 1850s. Death records at the county level for this period were not returned in any FamilySearch collection.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials), the 1852 California state census, and the 1860 federal census mortality schedule.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mission parishes, then diocesan parishes), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and others. The Diocese of Monterey (later San Francisco) covered California from the Mission era forward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. Mission registers are the oldest surviving series.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (collection 1804372, approximately 98,765 records) covers the Spanish/Mexican-era Franciscan mission registers through statehood. Gold Rush–era parish registers are held by individual parishes, diocesan archives, and the California State Archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed some of these.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Spanish and Latin. Later Catholic records may be in English, Irish (no), or reflect immigrant communities.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1850 federal census was the first taken in California, but it was **partially destroyed — some county returns are missing** (confirmed by the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). Do not treat a missing result as proof of absence. The 1860 census is intact and covers the full state.
- **State census:** The California state census of 1852 is the primary substitute for missing 1850 returns. FamilySearch holds a digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001) of 522 images, 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **indexed + images**. This is confirmed from volume_search results.
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850, 1860) record deaths in the year preceding the census and are available through FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census volume is indexed and online at FamilySearch. The 1860 federal census is indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories. Court files include naturalizations — all filed at the county level, as federal courts took over naturalization only in 1906.
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1850 onward.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for originals; some have been transferred to the California State Archives. The FamilySearch California Probate Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey — check the California State Archives website and individual county courthouses directly.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal land state using the rectangular survey (township/range) system for public-domain land. Pre-U.S. land grants from the Spanish and Mexican periods use metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government administered the public domain. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal patents. Pre-1848 Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) were adjudicated by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851 — these records are at the National Archives (San Bruno and Washington, D.C.).
- **Types:** Federal patents, county deed books, Spanish/Mexican land grant case files, tax records. Mining claims were not patents — they were registered at the county recorder's office of the county where the claim was located.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website for federal patents; county recorders for deeds and mining claims; NARA (San Bruno) for land grant case files.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848), California Indian Wars (1850s), Civil War (1861–1865 — California supplied Union regiments).
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; bounty land warrants (for Mexican War veterans); state adjutant general records at the California State Archives; California Union regiment records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and San Bruno); Fold3 for online access; California State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush–era cemeteries exist in every mining county; many are small, rural, or abandoned. Notable ones include Sacramento City Cemetery, Colma historic cemeteries (San Francisco area).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has extensive California coverage. BillionGraves also covers some cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; many early cemeteries have no formal registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Alta California (San Francisco, founded 1849) is the preeminent Gold Rush newspaper. Mining counties had their own papers (e.g., Nevada Journal, Stockton San Joaquin Republican). Many published death notices, probate legal notices, and mining news.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds historical newspapers; the California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) provides free access to many California papers; the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library hold physical microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, estate and probate legal notices, and mining claim disputes all appear in Gold Rush–era papers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary arrival port for sea-route migrants (around Cape Horn or via Panama). Some arrived overland; Sacramento was the primary interior terminus.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives (San Bruno, California). A digitized volume of Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento (1849–1858) exists on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images) but is **browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**. Naturalization records (pre-1906) are scattered across county and state courts.
- **Where held:** NARA San Bruno for passenger lists; FamilySearch for the browse-only Sacramento arrival volume; county courts for naturalization files.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including families traveling together. When researching a family arrival, examine the full manifest page for accompanying family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls. California also imposed a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, 1852) targeting non-U.S. miners — primarily affecting Chinese, Chilean, and Mexican miners.
- **Date range:** County tax records begin from county formation in 1850.
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and the California State Archives. Some are available on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can serve as a census substitute and can confirm presence in a county in a given year.

### Mining claim records
- **Types:** Mining claim registers filed at the county recorder's office of the county where the claim was located.
- **Where held:** A digitized volume of Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco (1849–1855) is on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images) but is **browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**. Original registers for other counties remain at county recorders' offices or the California State Archives.
- **Research value:** Mining claims name the claimant, describe the claim location, and sometimes name co-claimants or witnesses — useful for placing a miner in a specific locality.

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch collection "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (collection 1923340, approximately 1,345,678 records). These begin in 1866, after the target period, but capture many Gold Rush migrants who remained in California. They include physical description, occupation, and birthplace — among the most useful identification records for this cohort.
- **Overland trail records:** Diaries, journals, and emigrant registers document overland migrants. The California State Library and Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) hold extensive manuscript collections of Gold Rush–era personal papers, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); 1852 State Census volume (indexed); Mining Claim Registers and Sacramento Port Arrivals (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1850, 1860); mortality schedules | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers including Gold Rush era | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (service, pension, Civil War) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| CDNC (cdnc.ucr.edu) | California Digital Newspaper Collection | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for the 1848–1865 period in FamilySearch's holdings; the 3 detailed above are the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined. Request further pages before concluding the digitized set is exhausted.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives — San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco arrivals); Spanish/Mexican land grant case files | In-person / NARA research request |
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | County records transferred from courthouses; state agency records; adjutant general military records | In-person / online finding aids |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspaper microfilm; Great Registers originals | In-person / some digital |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush personal papers, diaries, journals | In-person by appointment |
| County courthouses | Deeds, mining claim registers, probate files, naturalizations, marriage licenses | In-person / mail request — varies by county |
| Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Monterey) | Post-1850 Catholic parish registers | Contact diocese directly |

## Records NOT online
- Most county-level probate case files for the 1850s remain in paper form at county courthouses or the California State Archives.
- Naturalization records filed in California county and state courts before 1906 are held at the filing court and are not fully digitized.
- Foreign Miners' Tax collection records are held at the California State Archives and are not indexed online.
- Most post-1850 Catholic parish registers for Gold Rush–era parishes are held by individual parishes or diocesan archives and are not broadly digitized.
- Mining claim registers for most counties (outside the San Francisco browse-only FamilySearch volume) remain at county recorders' offices.

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are entirely missing (confirmed by the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census is the primary substitute.
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed the San Francisco County Courthouse and many records held there, including some Gold Rush–era files. This primarily affects post-1865 records but researchers should be aware that some earlier records kept in San Francisco were lost.
- Many early mining camp and town records were never formally preserved and are simply absent.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census**, not the 1850 federal census, for Gold Rush migrants. The 1852 census (FamilySearch, volume 006601001, 88% indexed) was taken specifically to capture the rapidly changing population and covers people absent from or lost in the damaged 1850 returns. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **The California Genealogy wiki article** identifies ship passenger manifests at the National Archives San Bruno facility as a primary Gold Rush source, along with mining claim records at county recorders' offices. Use it as your orientation: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records
- **Identify the specific mining county** before searching county-level records. The Gold Rush counties (El Dorado, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Placer) each maintained separate records. A statewide search may miss browse-only volumes that are not name-indexed.
- **The Great Registers (1866–1910)** are essential for migrants who stayed in California past the target period. They record physical description, occupation, and nativity, making identification much more reliable than a name alone.
- **Search the Bancroft Library and California State Library** for personal papers, diaries, and letters, especially if your ancestor was literate. These institutions hold the largest collections of Gold Rush personal manuscripts anywhere. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **For Chinese, Chilean, and Mexican miners**, also consult the Foreign Miners' Tax records at the California State Archives, and be aware that Chinese community records (clan associations, tongs) maintained their own registers, some of which are held by Chinese-American historical societies.
