- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850, 1860) record deaths in the year preceding the census and are available through FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census volume is indexed and online at FamilySearch. The 1860 federal census is indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate estates), guardianships, inventories. Court files include naturalizations — all filed at the county level, as federal courts took over naturalization only in 1906.
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1850 onward.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for originals; some have been transferred to the California State Archives. The FamilySearch California Probate Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey — check the California State Archives website and individual county courthouses directly.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal land state using the rectangular survey (township/range) system for public-domain land. Pre-U.S. land grants from the Spanish and Mexican periods use metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government administered the public domain. The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal patents. Pre-1848 Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) were adjudicated by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851 — these records are at the National Archives (San Bruno and Washington, D.C.).
- **Types:** Federal patents, county deed books, Spanish/Mexican land grant case files, tax records. Mining claims were not patents — they were registered at the county recorder's office of the county where the claim was located.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website for federal patents; county recorders for deeds and mining claims; NARA (San Bruno) for land grant case files.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848), California Indian Wars (1850s), Civil War (1861–1865 — California supplied Union regiments).
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; bounty land warrants (for Mexican War veterans); state adjutant general records at the California State Archives; California Union regiment records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and San Bruno); Fold3 for online access; California State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Gold Rush–era cemeteries exist in every mining county; many are small, rural, or abandoned. Notable ones include Sacramento City Cemetery, Colma historic cemeteries (San Francisco area).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has extensive California coverage. BillionGraves also covers some cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; many early cemeteries have no formal registers.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Alta California (San Francisco, founded 1849) is the preeminent Gold Rush newspaper. Mining counties had their own papers (e.g., Nevada Journal, Stockton San Joaquin Republican). Many published death notices, probate legal notices, and mining news.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds historical newspapers; the California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) provides free access to many California papers; the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library hold physical microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, estate and probate legal notices, and mining claim disputes all appear in Gold Rush–era papers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** San Francisco was the primary arrival port for sea-route migrants (around Cape Horn or via Panama). Some arrived overland; Sacramento was the primary interior terminus.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives (San Bruno, California). A digitized volume of Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento (1849–1858) exists on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images) but is **browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**. Naturalization records (pre-1906) are scattered across county and state courts.
- **Where held:** NARA San Bruno for passenger lists; FamilySearch for the browse-only Sacramento arrival volume; county courts for naturalization files.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including families traveling together. When researching a family arrival, examine the full manifest page for accompanying family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment rolls. California also imposed a Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, 1852) targeting non-U.S. miners — primarily affecting Chinese, Chilean, and Mexican miners.
- **Date range:** County tax records begin from county formation in 1850.
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and the California State Archives. Some are available on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can serve as a census substitute and can confirm presence in a county in a given year.

### Mining claim records
- **Types:** Mining claim registers filed at the county recorder's office of the county where the claim was located.
- **Where held:** A digitized volume of Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco (1849–1855) is on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images) but is **browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**. Original registers for other counties remain at county recorders' offices or the California State Archives.
- **Research value:** Mining claims name the claimant, describe the claim location, and sometimes name co-claimants or witnesses — useful for placing a miner in a specific locality.

### Other record types
- **Great Registers (voter registration):** FamilySearch collection "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" (collection 1923340, approximately 1,345,678 records). These begin in 1866, after the target period, but capture many Gold Rush migrants who remained in California. They include physical description, occupation, and birthplace — among the most useful identification records for this cohort.
- **Overland trail records:** Diaries, journals, and emigrant registers document overland migrants. The California State Library and Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) hold extensive manuscript collections of Gold Rush–era personal papers, per the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); 1852 State Census volume (indexed); Mining Claim Registers and Sacramento Port Arrivals (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1850, 1860); mortality schedules | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical California newspapers including Gold Rush era | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (service, pension, Civil War) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for California | Free |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records statewide | Free |
| CDNC (cdnc.ucr.edu) | California Digital Newspaper Collection | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for the 1848–1865 period in FamilySearch's holdings; the 3 detailed above are the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined. Request further pages before concluding the digitized set is exhausted.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives — San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco arrivals); Spanish/Mexican land grant case files | In-person / NARA research request |
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | County records transferred from courthouses; state agency records; adjutant general military records | In-person / online finding aids |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | Gold Rush manuscript collections; newspaper microfilm; Great Registers originals | In-person / some digital |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Extensive Gold Rush personal papers, diaries, journals | In-person by appointment |
| County courthouses | Deeds, mining claim registers, probate files, naturalizations, marriage licenses | In-person / mail request — varies by county |
| Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Monterey) | Post-1850 Catholic parish registers | Contact diocese directly |

## Records NOT online
- Most county-level probate case files for the 1850s remain in paper form at county courthouses or the California State Archives.
- Naturalization records filed in California county and state courts before 1906 are held at the filing court and are not fully digitized.
- Foreign Miners' Tax collection records are held at the California State Archives and are not indexed online.
- Most post-1850 Catholic parish registers for Gold Rush–era parishes are held by individual parishes or diocesan archives and are not broadly digitized.
- Mining claim registers for most counties (outside the San Francisco browse-only FamilySearch volume) remain at county recorders' offices.

## Known record losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are entirely missing (confirmed by the FamilySearch California Genealogy wiki article at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records). The 1852 California state census is the primary substitute.
- The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed the San Francisco County Courthouse and many records held there, including some Gold Rush–era files. This primarily affects post-1865 records but researchers should be aware that some earlier records kept in San Francisco were lost.
- Many early mining camp and town records were never formally preserved and are simply absent.

## Research tips
- **Start with the 1852 California state census**, not the 1850 federal census, for Gold Rush migrants. The 1852 census (FamilySearch, volume 006601001, 88% indexed) was taken specifically to capture the rapidly changing population and covers people absent from or lost in the damaged 1850 returns. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **The California Genealogy wiki article** identifies ship passenger manifests at the National Archives San Bruno facility as a primary Gold Rush source, along with mining claim records at county recorders' offices. Use it as your orientation: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records
- **Identify the specific mining county** before searching county-level records. The Gold Rush counties (El Dorado, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Placer) each maintained separate records. A statewide search may miss browse-only volumes that are not name-indexed.
- **The Great Registers (1866–1910)** are essential for migrants who stayed in California past the target period. They record physical description, occupation, and nativity, making identification much more reliable than a name alone.
- **Search the Bancroft Library and California State Library** for personal papers, diaries, and letters, especially if your ancestor was literate. These institutions hold the largest collections of Gold Rush personal manuscripts anywhere. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **For Chinese, Chilean, and Mexican miners**, also consult the Foreign Miners' Tax records at the California State Archives, and be aware that Chinese community records (clan associations, tongs) maintained their own registers, some of which are held by Chinese-American historical societies.

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001** in `research.json`.

---

Researching New York City families in the 1700s colonial period means working in a world without civil birth, marriage, or death records — those did not exist in colonial New York. The most important records are church registers, particularly those of the Dutch Reformed congregation (whose registers survive from 1639 and are partly on FamilySearch, though in Dutch and browseable only image by image), and the Anglican Trinity Church (from 1698). Probate records exist through the province-wide Prerogative Court of New York, indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* published by the New-York Historical Society. Land records, ward-level tax lists, militia rolls, and colonial manuscripts at the New York State Archives round out what survives.

A critical point: "New York City" in the 1700s meant Manhattan (New York County) only — ancestors in Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, or the Bronx were recorded under Kings, Queens, Richmond, or Westchester County respectively, and those must be researched separately.

**Key record types and where to find them:**

- **Dutch Reformed Church registers** (from 1639) — FamilySearch (partially digitized, in Dutch, image-only browsing) and the New-York Historical Society
- **Trinity Church (Anglican) records** (from 1698) — NYGBS and FamilySearch
- **Probate records** — Prerogative Court of New York; indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* (NYHS); FamilySearch has digitized probate collections
- **Land records** — New York State Archives and FamilySearch
- **Ward-level tax lists and militia rolls** — New York State Archives and New-York Historical Society
- **Colonial manuscripts** — New York State Archives (Albany)

**Primary repositories:**
- New York City Municipal Archives
- New York State Archives (Albany)
- New-York Historical Society
- New York Genealogical and Biographical Society (NYGBS)
- FamilySearch (five digitized New York collections overlapping the 1700s)

With this locality guide in place, the logical next step is building a targeted research plan — identifying the specific record sets most likely to document your named ancestor, and the order in which to search them.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (New York County), Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Dutch colony of New Amsterdam established 1626; seized by England 1664 and renamed New York.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City (Manhattan Island), seat of New York County and capital of New York Province.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British Crown colony, 1664–1783); became New York State 1788.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tools for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport and trading hub; merchant commerce dominant (Wikipedia, New York City article).
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, French Huguenot, German, African (enslaved and free), and other European settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), and others — per wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Key historical events:** English takeover from Dutch 1664; French and Indian War 1754–1763; American Revolution 1775–1783, including British military occupation of New York City 1776–1783.

## Boundary changes
- Colonial 'New York City' was coextensive with Manhattan Island, organized as New York County.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Virginia during the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is among the best-documented American colonial jurisdictions. The Commonwealth kept records at the county level from the 1630s, so the key to finding any family is identifying which county they lived in year by year. Here is a survey of the most valuable records and repositories:

---

## Military Service Records

- **Continental Army service records and muster rolls** — National Archives, Record Group 93. These document soldiers who served in the Continental Army, listing name, rank, unit, and sometimes physical description.
- **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia (Richmond). Virginia raised extensive militia forces; muster rolls, pay vouchers, and officer rosters survive for most counties.
- **Pension application files** — National Archives, Record Group 15. These are especially valuable: veterans and widows filed sworn statements *decades* after the war detailing family history, marriage dates, and military service. Many are digitized on Fold3 and FamilySearch.
- **Virginia bounty land warrants and surveys** — Library of Virginia. Veterans who received Virginia bounty land grants in the Virginia Military District of Ohio left warrant and survey records here, separate from any federal bounty land warrants.

---

## Home-Front Records (Families Not in Military)

- **1782–1785 county personal property tax lists** — These are the single most important substitute for the 1790 federal census (which was lost when the British burned Washington in 1814). Indexed on FamilySearch, collection 1456723.
- **County court records** — Land deeds, wills, estates, and court minutes from individual Virginia counties. Each county courthouse or its records at the Library of Virginia holds these.

---

## Vital and Church Records

- **Anglican (Episcopal) vestry books** — Virginia had no statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in this period. Anglican vestry books are the nearest equivalent and survive for many parishes. The Library of Virginia holds many originals and microfilm copies.
- **Dissenting church registers** (Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist) — As Virginia's religious diversity grew in the Revolutionary era, these denominations kept their own registers; survival is uneven but worth checking.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia**, Richmond (lva.virginia.gov) | Militia records, county court records, vestry books, bounty land warrants, tax lists |
| **National Archives** (archives.gov) | Continental service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15), federal bounty land warrants |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Digitized copies of tax lists, some militia records, pension index |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Digitized pension applications, compiled military service records |
| **DAR (Daughters of the American Revolution)** | Compiled patriot indexes and lineage records; useful for locating existing research |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the county first.** Virginia's records are county-based; knowing where the family lived is essential before searching any specific record type.
2. **Check the pension files even for non-veterans.** Widows and heirs filed, and these narratives often name children, neighbors, and the county of residence.
3. **Use the 1782–1785 tax lists as a census substitute.** They list free white males by name and sometimes personal property, providing a snapshot of the wartime household.
4. **Look for compilations.** John Vogt and T. William Kethley's *Virginia Tax Records* and Netti Schreiner-Yantis's compiled indexes are widely used finding aids.

---

With this locality guide saved, the logical next step is a **research plan** that sequences these sources into a specific search strategy for your ancestor or family line. If you share the name and county of the ancestor you're tracing, I can help build that plan.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; became the Commonwealth of Virginia in 1776 upon independence
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; previously Williamsburg)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population figures for 1775-1783 were not returned by tools for this survey period
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming, maritime trade; war disrupted the plantation economy across Tidewater and Piedmont
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descended majority; substantial African American (enslaved) population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in western counties; Loyalist minority throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Church of England (Anglican/Episcopal) was the established church through 1785; Presbyterians, Baptists, Quakers, Lutherans, and Methodists (late in the period) also present
- **Key historical events:** Virginia Convention and Declaration of Independence (1776); major battles and campaigns on Virginia soil including the Siege of Yorktown (1781); disruption of county operations in areas of active military activity

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's territory was vast in this period, encompassing what is now Kentucky and West Virginia; West Virginia did not separate until 1863
- Kentucky County was formed from Fincastle County in 1776, then divided into Fayette, Jefferson, and Lincoln counties in 1780; ancestors in present-day Kentucky were under Virginia county jurisdiction throughout this period — their records are Virginia county records
- Numerous new counties were formed in Virginia's western territories during the 1770s-1780s as settlement expanded; identifying the correct county of residence for each specific year is essential
- The `place_search_all` tool returned no jurisdictional data for this survey; verify any boundary question against the Library of Virginia's county formation records

## Available record types

**Note on all record levels:** Virginia had no statewide civil registration during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records and Church Records returned only generic content during this survey; no Virginia-specific registration dates were returned. Do not assume civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period. The statements below reflect what the tools returned.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content — no Virginia-specific start date was returned by any tool in this survey.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level by county clerks; some survive from the colonial period through the Revolution. No civil birth or death registration existed at any level during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriage bonds and licenses); Library of Virginia holds many microfilmed county records
- **Gaps:** War disrupted some county court operations, particularly in Tidewater and Southside; courthouse fires in later decades destroyed some early records
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican vestry books and parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); probate records (naming heirs and family members); county court order books

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England/Anglican (established church through 1785); Quakers; Presbyterians; Baptists; Lutherans; German Reformed; Methodists (arriving late in the period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Anglican vestry minutes (which also recorded poor relief and parish business naming many local people); communion rolls
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, 1,234,567 records); Library of Virginia; individual denominational archives; Virginia Historical Society
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census in 1790 is the closest to this period; however, the 1790 Virginia schedules were entirely destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — no 1790 federal census exists for Virginia
- **State/provincial census:** No state census during 1775-1783
- **Other enumerations:** County personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723, "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850", 456,789 records) and land tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census. One digitized volume of state enumerations and tax lists (1782-1799) is available on FamilySearch (DGS 005301449, 87 images); this volume is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — it must be searched using full-text tools, not a surname index, and browsed image by image
- **Access:** The Tax Records collection (1456723) is name-indexed on FamilySearch. Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable only (no name index)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships, and county court order books (which recorded road maintenance, debt suits, apprenticeship indentures, poor relief, and county business beyond lawsuits)
- **Testate or intestate:** Search will books for testate estates (wills); search administration books for intestate estates (no will). Guardianship filings after a soldier's death name surviving minor children by name and age.
- **Date range:** County courts operated continuously; records survive from the 1630s in the oldest counties. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, 1,789,012 records) covers the period. One digitized volume of Augusta County court order books, 1775-1795 (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed) is available.
- **Where held:** Original records at county courthouses and Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 2134567 and volume 005301448 online

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia colonial land patents were issued by the Crown through the Governor's Council; after independence, the Virginia General Land Office issued grants. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Virginia Land and Property — consult the Library of Virginia directly for land grant records.
- **Types:** Land patents and grants; deed books at county courthouses; mortgage records; bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio (for veterans)
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, 2,567,890 records) covers the full period. Bounty land warrant records (DGS 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) are digitized but browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- **Where held:** County deed books at county courthouses and Library of Virginia; Virginia Military District of Ohio warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783). Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15 (among the richest genealogical sources — filed decades later, often containing the veteran's own sworn narrative, witnesses, and widow's pension applications with marriage date and place)
  - Virginia State Navy records
  - Bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio: Library of Virginia and FamilySearch (DGS 005301447, 341 images, browse-only)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, 345,678 records, indexed); Fold3 (www.fold3.com, subscription)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 1945678 is name-indexed. Pension files at NARA are accessible through Fold3 (subscription) and some are digitized at Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era church graveyards throughout the state; family farm cemeteries; plantation burial grounds; many Revolutionary-era graves are unmarked or have lost markers
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many Virginia cemetery transcriptions; some church cemetery records are included in Virginia Church Records collection (1598230)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, when they survive, are held by individual churches or have been transferred to the Library of Virginia

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published during the colonial and Revolutionary period; wartime publication was intermittent
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription); Library of Virginia newspaper collections; Virginia Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), military notices, and other announcements name individuals and family members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk, Alexandria, and Yorktown (before and after the war); severely disrupted by the British naval blockade during the conflict
- **Record types:** Pre-war passenger lists from British ports; post-war arrivals at Virginia ports; Loyalist emigration records; declarations of intention and early naturalization records in county courts
- **Where held:** NARA; Library of Virginia; UK National Archives, Kew (for Loyalist claims and pre-war colonial arrivals)
- **Content note:** The war significantly disrupted immigration; most immigration records useful for this period relate to the pre-war colonial era or the post-war Federal period. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — when examining a family arrival, check the full manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax lists and land tax lists, both assessed annually at the county level from 1782
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, 456,789 records); digitized volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists, 1782-1799, 87 images)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (indexed collection 1456723; full-text-searchable volume 005301449)
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed, the 1782-1785 personal property tax lists are the single most important substitute census source for Virginia Revolutionary War-era research

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Confiscated Loyalist estates generated court proceedings, land records, and personal property inventories — essential for Loyalist families and those caught between sides
- **County court order books:** Record road maintenance assignments, debt suits, apprenticeship indentures, poor relief, and county business — naming many people absent from other record series
- **Post-war pension files:** Revolutionary War pension applications filed from the 1790s through the 1830s are among the richest genealogical sources; they contain sworn affidavits, marriage statements, and family declarations. Access via NARA RG 15, Fold3, and Ancestry.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (345,678 records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (456,789 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1,234,567 records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (2,567,890 records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (1,789,012 records) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Census, military, land, and vital records for Virginia | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Continental Army records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free finding aids; some free digitized records |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia, 1775-1800 — the complete result set (no further pages). No volume summary was returned. The `collections_search` returned 5 indexed collections for Virginia.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Virginia militia records, land grant records, county deed books, wills, tax lists, state archives | In-person; many records microfilmed and on FamilySearch |
| National Archives (Washington DC) | Continental Army records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | In-person or via Fold3 and Ancestry online |
| Virginia County Courthouses | Deed books, will books, order books, marriage bonds — originals | In-person or mail requests |
| Virginia Historical Society (Richmond) | Manuscript collections, family papers, church records | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Original Virginia militia muster rolls and pay vouchers at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized
- Most county deed books and will books exist only on microfilm or as physical volumes at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia
- Loyalist claims records are held at the UK National Archives, Kew, and are not fully digitized
- Vestry books of smaller Anglican parishes may exist only at individual churches or the Virginia Diocesan archives
- Virginia State Navy records are not fully indexed or digitized
- Bounty land warrant records (DGS 005301447) are digitized images but have no name index and are not full-text searchable — physical browsing of 341 images required

## Known record losses

- **1790 federal census destroyed:** The Virginia schedules from the first federal census (1790) were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782-1785 county tax lists are the essential substitute.
- **Courthouse fires:** Numerous Virginia county courthouses suffered fires during the 19th century; counties with significant record losses include Gloucester (1820) and Charles City, among others. Early records in affected jurisdictions may be fragmentary.
- **Wartime disruption:** County court operations were disrupted in areas of active military operations (Tidewater, Southside) during the war, which may have created gaps in routine recording.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the Virginia-specific pages (Vital Records, Military Records, Land, Church) all returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly before relying on their absence.
- Virginia militia records are held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond; per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), contact or visit the Library of Virginia directly for militia muster rolls and pay vouchers not yet digitized.
- For any soldier who survived the war: always search for a pension application (NARA RG 15, accessible via Fold3). These files — often filed decades later — contain the most detailed genealogical information, including the soldier's sworn narrative, witnesses' affidavits, and the widow's pension application with a stated marriage date and place.
- County tax lists from the 1780s are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census; begin your search for this period with the personal property tax lists in FamilySearch collection 1456723, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- Virginia bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio are separate from federal bounty land warrants — a veteran could hold both; Virginia warrants are at the Library of Virginia and the federal warrants are at NARA.
- County of residence during the war is the key to finding records: identify which county your ancestor lived in for each year, and determine whether that county was formed from a parent county during the period — pre-formation records will be in the parent county's deed and order books.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; became the Commonwealth of Virginia in 1776 upon independence
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; previously Williamsburg)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of Great Britain until 1776; Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population figures for 1775-1783 were not returned by tools for this survey period
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming, maritime trade; war disrupted the plantation economy across Tidewater and Piedmont
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descended majority; substantial African American (enslaved) population; Scots-Irish and German settlers in western counties; Loyalist minority throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Church of England (Anglican/Episcopal) was the established church through 1785; Presbyterians, Baptists, Quakers, Lutherans, and Methodists (late in the period) also present
- **Key historical events:** Virginia Convention and Declaration of Independence (1776); major battles and campaigns on Virginia soil including the Siege of Yorktown (1781); disruption of county operations in areas of active military activity

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's territory was vast in this period, encompassing what is now Kentucky and West Virginia; West Virginia did not separate until 1863
- Kentucky County was formed from Fincastle County in 1776, then divided into Fayette, Jefferson, and Lincoln counties in 1780; ancestors in present-day Kentucky were under Virginia county jurisdiction throughout this period — their records are Virginia county records
- Numerous new counties were formed in Virginia's western territories during the 1770s-1780s as settlement expanded; identifying the correct county of residence for each specific year is essential
- The `place_search_all` tool returned no jurisdictional data for this survey; verify any boundary question against the Library of Virginia's county formation records

## Available record types

**Note on all record levels:** Virginia had no statewide civil registration during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records and Church Records returned only generic content during this survey; no Virginia-specific registration dates were returned. Do not assume civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period. The statements below reflect what the tools returned.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content — no Virginia-specific start date was returned by any tool in this survey.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level by county clerks; some survive from the colonial period through the Revolution. No civil birth or death registration existed at any level during this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (marriage bonds and licenses); Library of Virginia holds many microfilmed county records
- **Gaps:** War disrupted some county court operations, particularly in Tidewater and Southside; courthouse fires in later decades destroyed some early records
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican vestry books and parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials); probate records (naming heirs and family members); county court order books

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England/Anglican (established church through 1785); Quakers; Presbyterians; Baptists; Lutherans; German Reformed; Methodists (arriving late in the period)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Anglican vestry minutes (which also recorded poor relief and parish business naming many local people); communion rolls
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, 1,234,567 records); Library of Virginia; individual denominational archives; Virginia Historical Society
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census in 1790 is the closest to this period; however, the 1790 Virginia schedules were entirely destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — no 1790 federal census exists for Virginia
- **State/provincial census:** No state census during 1775-1783
- **Other enumerations:** County personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723, "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850", 456,789 records) and land tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census. One digitized volume of state enumerations and tax lists (1782-1799) is available on FamilySearch (DGS 005301449, 87 images); this volume is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — it must be searched using full-text tools, not a surname index, and browsed image by image
- **Access:** The Tax Records collection (1456723) is name-indexed on FamilySearch. Volume 005301449 is full-text searchable only (no name index)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships, and county court order books (which recorded road maintenance, debt suits, apprenticeship indentures, poor relief, and county business beyond lawsuits)
- **Testate or intestate:** Search will books for testate estates (wills); search administration books for intestate estates (no will). Guardianship filings after a soldier's death name surviving minor children by name and age.
- **Date range:** County courts operated continuously; records survive from the 1630s in the oldest counties. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, 1,789,012 records) covers the period. One digitized volume of Augusta County court order books, 1775-1795 (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed) is available.
- **Where held:** Original records at county courthouses and Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection 2134567 and volume 005301448 online

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Virginia colonial land patents were issued by the Crown through the Governor's Council; after independence, the Virginia General Land Office issued grants. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Virginia Land and Property — consult the Library of Virginia directly for land grant records.
- **Types:** Land patents and grants; deed books at county courthouses; mortgage records; bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio (for veterans)
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, 2,567,890 records) covers the full period. Bounty land warrant records (DGS 005301447, 341 images, 1779-1800) are digitized but browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- **Where held:** County deed books at county courthouses and Library of Virginia; Virginia Military District of Ohio warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783). Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Record types:**
  - Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93
  - Virginia militia records: Library of Virginia, Richmond
  - Pension and bounty-land warrant application files: NARA Record Group 15 (among the richest genealogical sources — filed decades later, often containing the veteran's own sworn narrative, witnesses, and widow's pension applications with marriage date and place)
  - Virginia State Navy records
  - Bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio: Library of Virginia and FamilySearch (DGS 005301447, 341 images, browse-only)
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC); Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, 345,678 records, indexed); Fold3 (www.fold3.com, subscription)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection 1945678 is name-indexed. Pension files at NARA are accessible through Fold3 (subscription) and some are digitized at Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Colonial-era church graveyards throughout the state; family farm cemeteries; plantation burial grounds; many Revolutionary-era graves are unmarked or have lost markers
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) indexes many Virginia cemetery transcriptions; some church cemetery records are included in Virginia Church Records collection (1598230)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, when they survive, are held by individual churches or have been transferred to the Library of Virginia

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published during the colonial and Revolutionary period; wartime publication was intermittent
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription); Library of Virginia newspaper collections; Virginia Historical Society
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), military notices, and other announcements name individuals and family members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk, Alexandria, and Yorktown (before and after the war); severely disrupted by the British naval blockade during the conflict
- **Record types:** Pre-war passenger lists from British ports; post-war arrivals at Virginia ports; Loyalist emigration records; declarations of intention and early naturalization records in county courts
- **Where held:** NARA; Library of Virginia; UK National Archives, Kew (for Loyalist claims and pre-war colonial arrivals)
- **Content note:** The war significantly disrupted immigration; most immigration records useful for this period relate to the pre-war colonial era or the post-war Federal period. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — when examining a family arrival, check the full manifest.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax lists and land tax lists, both assessed annually at the county level from 1782
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, 456,789 records); digitized volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists, 1782-1799, 87 images)
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (indexed collection 1456723; full-text-searchable volume 005301449)
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed, the 1782-1785 personal property tax lists are the single most important substitute census source for Virginia Revolutionary War-era research

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** Confiscated Loyalist estates generated court proceedings, land records, and personal property inventories — essential for Loyalist families and those caught between sides
- **County court order books:** Record road maintenance assignments, debt suits, apprenticeship indentures, poor relief, and county business — naming many people absent from other record series
- **Post-war pension files:** Revolutionary War pension applications filed from the 1790s through the 1830s are among the richest genealogical sources; they contain sworn affidavits, marriage statements, and family declarations. Access via NARA RG 15, Fold3, and Ancestry.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (345,678 records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (456,789 records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1,234,567 records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (2,567,890 records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (1,789,012 records) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Census, military, land, and vital records for Virginia | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions statewide | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Continental Army records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free finding aids; some free digitized records |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia, 1775-1800 — the complete result set (no further pages). No volume summary was returned. The `collections_search` returned 5 indexed collections for Virginia.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Virginia militia records, land grant records, county deed books, wills, tax lists, state archives | In-person; many records microfilmed and on FamilySearch |
| National Archives (Washington DC) | Continental Army records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | In-person or via Fold3 and Ancestry online |
| Virginia County Courthouses | Deed books, will books, order books, marriage bonds — originals | In-person or mail requests |
| Virginia Historical Society (Richmond) | Manuscript collections, family papers, church records | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Original Virginia militia muster rolls and pay vouchers at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized
- Most county deed books and will books exist only on microfilm or as physical volumes at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia
- Loyalist claims records are held at the UK National Archives, Kew, and are not fully digitized
- Vestry books of smaller Anglican parishes may exist only at individual churches or the Virginia Diocesan archives
- Virginia State Navy records are not fully indexed or digitized
- Bounty land warrant records (DGS 005301447) are digitized images but have no name index and are not full-text searchable — physical browsing of 341 images required

## Known record losses

- **1790 federal census destroyed:** The Virginia schedules from the first federal census (1790) were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The 1782-1785 county tax lists are the essential substitute.
- **Courthouse fires:** Numerous Virginia county courthouses suffered fires during the 19th century; counties with significant record losses include Gloucester (1820) and Charles City, among others. Early records in affected jurisdictions may be fragmentary.
- **Wartime disruption:** County court operations were disrupted in areas of active military operations (Tidewater, Southside) during the war, which may have created gaps in routine recording.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the Virginia-specific pages (Vital Records, Military Records, Land, Church) all returned only generic content during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly before relying on their absence.
- Virginia militia records are held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond; per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War), contact or visit the Library of Virginia directly for militia muster rolls and pay vouchers not yet digitized.
- For any soldier who survived the war: always search for a pension application (NARA RG 15, accessible via Fold3). These files — often filed decades later — contain the most detailed genealogical information, including the soldier's sworn narrative, witnesses' affidavits, and the widow's pension application with a stated marriage date and place.
- County tax lists from the 1780s are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census; begin your search for this period with the personal property tax lists in FamilySearch collection 1456723, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- Virginia bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio are separate from federal bounty land warrants — a veteran could hold both; Virginia warrants are at the Library of Virginia and the federal warrants are at NARA.
- County of residence during the war is the key to finding records: identify which county your ancestor lived in for each year, and determine whether that county was formed from a parent county during the period — pre-formation records will be in the parent county's deed and order books.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide's response for early-1800s New Orleans:

---

Researching ancestors in early-1800s New Orleans means working around **two catastrophic fires** — in **1788 and 1794** — that destroyed most of the French Quarter and the bulk of colonial records. What survived and remained usable through the early 1800s falls into two main categories:

### Records That Survived

1. **St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps). These are the primary source for births and pre-1837 marriages. Records appear in French, Spanish, and English depending on the date.

2. **Notarial Archives** — over 30 million pages of legal acts dating to 1734, held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**. Because Louisiana follows civil law, notarial acts recorded property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions, apprenticeships, and much else that other states handled through deeds, wills, and courts. This is the single most important repository to consult before concluding someone left no records.

### Where to Look

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (digitized) | Church records 1718–1925, parish marriages 1837–1957, probate records 1756–1984, death index from 1819, and a small browse-only volume of notarial acts 1803–1820 |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | The main notarial act collection (in person or by mail) |
| **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge** | Statewide records and civil registration |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Church sacramental registers |

### Key Warnings for This Period

- **Civil registration did not begin in Louisiana until 1837** — for births and pre-1837 marriages, the church register collection is your primary source, not a civil register series.
- For **any community** in New Orleans (free persons of color, enslaved individuals, French Creoles, Spanish colonists, Anglo-Americans), notarial acts often capture transactions and relationships that appear nowhere else.
- The next practical step is to build a research plan targeting the specific ancestors and record types most likely to survive for your family's community during this period.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1718, founded by the French; under Spanish colonial authority 1763–1800; briefly returned to France before the Louisiana Purchase in 1803; Orleans Territory 1803–1812; City of New Orleans within Orleans Parish, State of Louisiana from 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of Orleans Parish).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Parish, Louisiana; Louisiana was a U.S. state from 1812; a U.S. territory 1803–1812.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place-population tool for this survey.
- **Economy:** Major port and commercial hub; sugar and cotton trade; Mississippi River commerce dominated economic life and drew heavy immigrant traffic.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), and a large enslaved population; German, Irish, and Italian immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1820. This diversity shapes records — registers were kept in French, Spanish, and English across the period.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic dominant (St. Louis Cathedral, established 1718); Protestant congregations grew after the Louisiana Purchase; Jewish congregations present by 1820.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815 (War of 1812); repeated yellow fever epidemics (1853 was catastrophic); hurricanes and floods throughout the period. Critically, two fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and large volumes of colonial records — their effect is felt through the entire early-1800s research period.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans was governed under French and then Spanish colonial law before 1803. Records from those regimes were created under different administrative systems and are now split between the New Orleans Notarial Archives, the Louisiana State Archives, and the Archdiocese of New Orleans archives.
- After the Louisiana Purchase (1803), the city was part of Orleans Territory until Louisiana statehood on 18 April 1812. Territorial-era records (1803–1812) may be filed as Orleans Territory rather than Louisiana State records — search both designations.
- Orleans Parish boundaries have encompassed the City of New Orleans throughout the period; the city and parish are coextensive. There is no separate county structure.

## Known record losses

This is the most critical context for early-1800s New Orleans research:

- **Great Fire of 21 March 1788:** Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter. Many civil and ecclesiastical records were consumed. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)), this fire and the second fire of 1794 together destroyed most of the colonial-era records of the French Quarter.
- **Fire of 8 December 1794:** A second major fire destroyed another 212 buildings and additional records.
- **Subsequent water and climate damage:** Wikipedia notes that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings across the nineteenth century.
- **Implication for researchers:** The absence of a record for events before approximately 1795 should default to assumed fire loss, not evidence that the event did not occur. Substitute sources and surviving series are described below.

## What survived and where it is

Despite the fires, significant sources survive for the early 1800s. The FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)) identifies the following as the core survivors:

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, though with gaps caused by the fires. These are the primary vital-event source for the early 1800s.
2. **Notarial acts** — The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC) holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734. Notarial records in Louisiana's civil-law system recorded transactions that common-law states handled in deeds, contracts, and courts — property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions, apprenticeships, and business agreements all appear here.
3. **Cabildo records** — The records of the Spanish colonial governing body survived in part and are held at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; no specific civil-registration start date or level can be cited from a tool result. Do not assume statewide registration existed during 1800–1860 — for most of the United States this period predates mandatory registration.
- **What exists for this period:** No indexed civil-registration collections covering 1800–1860 were returned by FamilySearch collections search. The primary vital-event records for this period are the church sacramental registers (see Church Records below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731+); the FamilySearch collection *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925* (collection 1612905, 987,654 records with images).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant); Protestant and Jewish congregations growing after 1803.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations — recorded by St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 (with gaps from the fires).
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925* (collection 1612905) — 987,654 records with 493,827 images, indexed + images, accessible free at FamilySearch.org.
- **Language:** Records are in French and/or Spanish through approximately 1810; English appears alongside French thereafter. Researchers must be prepared to read records in those languages or use transcriptions cautiously.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch microfilm and digitized collection 1612905.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was enumerated beginning in 1810 (as a state from 1812). Federal censuses for 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, and 1860 all cover New Orleans. The 1890 census was destroyed by fire nationally — not a New Orleans-specific loss.
- **State/territorial census:** No Louisiana-specific territorial or state census collections were returned by this survey's tools.
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). 1850 and 1860 include individual names for all free persons; earlier censuses list heads of household only.

### Notarial records
- **Types:** Property sales, marriage contracts, manumissions of enslaved persons, apprenticeship contracts, business agreements, wills drafted before a notary, successions (probate inventories), and more. In Louisiana's civil-law system, notarial acts substitute for most record types that other states produced in different courts or offices.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004990115 — 167 images, covering Orleans, Louisiana 1803–1820, labeled "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)". Digitization level: **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable); in French and English; must be examined image by image.
- **Physical repository:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC) — holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734. This is the largest collection of notarial records in the United States and far exceeds what is on FamilySearch.
- **Access to NONARC:** In-person at 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans; partial online index at notarialarchives.org.

### Probate records
- **Louisiana terminology:** Probate is called "successions"; guardianship is "tutorship"; interdictions (incompetency proceedings) are a third type unique to civil law.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984* (collection 2078341) — 456,789 records with 228,394 images, indexed + images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge.

### Land records
- **Survey system and law:** Civil law (Napoleonic Code). Land transactions were notarial acts, not common-law deeds. The relevant repository is the NONARC, not a county deed office.
- **Federal land grants:** After the Louisiana Purchase, the U.S. General Land Office issued patents for federal lands. GLO records are searchable at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Spanish land grants:** Some Spanish colonial land grants affecting New Orleans-area property survive at the Louisiana State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812, culminating in the Battle of New Orleans (8 January 1815); Mexican-American War 1846–1848 (Louisiana troops participated); early Civil War activity 1861 (just outside the period).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants — at the National Archives (NARA), searchable via Fold3 (subscription).
- **Louisiana State Archives:** May hold state militia records for the territorial and early statehood period.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833) — all active during 1800–1860.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and BillionGraves have partial coverage; above-ground vault burials in New Orleans mean inscriptions may survive where in-ground stones have not.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records and burial registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (from 1794), *Louisiana Gazette* (from 1804), *New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille* (from 1827), *Daily Picayune* (from 1837). Papers were often bilingual (French/English).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america) have partial digitized runs. Physical microfilm at the New Orleans Public Library and the Louisiana State University Libraries.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale notices, sheriff's sales, naturalization declarations, and notices of free-person-of-color registration.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Port significance:** New Orleans was the second-busiest port of entry in the United States during 1800–1860, behind only New York. Passenger lists are a primary source for immigrant ancestors.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed in Orleans Parish courts, pre-1906 in any court of record); alien registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Orleans Parish Civil District Court or U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana (naturalizations).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. Examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.
- **Inland naturalization:** Declarations of intention could be filed in any court, so a person who arrived at New Orleans may have naturalized in a county or parish court far from the port.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Orleans Parish property tax and personal property tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax rolls survive from the territorial period (1803+).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Louisiana Collection, Tulane University.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place a person in New Orleans in years between census enumerations and can document property ownership when deeds (notarial acts) are missing.

### Enslaved persons records
- **Types:** Manumission acts (notarial records at NONARC), succession inventories listing enslaved persons by name, bills of sale (notarial acts), baptismal records at St. Louis Cathedral (enslaved people were baptized), and separate registers of free people of color.
- **Free persons of color:** Louisiana maintained a legally distinct category of free people of color who were required to register; these registers survive at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Access:** NONARC for notarial acts; FamilySearch collection 1612905 for baptismal records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records + images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (567,890 records + images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records + images); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 index entries, no images); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (004990115, 1803-1820, 167 images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1810-1860 for Louisiana); passenger lists; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files, War of 1812 records | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Partial digitized runs of New Orleans newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans, Louisiana 1800–1820 (the query's internal end year was 1820, not 1860). For 1820–1860, no further digitized volumes were returned. The single volume is browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC) | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734+ | In-person at 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans; partial index at notarialarchives.org |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records; Cabildo records; tax rolls; free-persons-of-color registers; Louisiana Statewide Death Index underlying records | In-person or mail request; some collections online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731+); other parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) files; guardianship (tutorship) records; court minutes | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Newspaper microfilm; city directories; local history collections | In-person |
| Tulane University, Louisiana Collection | Manuscript collections; plantation records; newspaper runs | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records including naturalization petitions; U.S. District Court Eastern Louisiana | In-person or NARA online access |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages, 1734+) is not digitized or indexed online; only the single browse-only FamilySearch volume (004990115, 167 images, 1803-1820) exists digitally.
- St. Louis Cathedral registers beyond what is captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 must be consulted through the Archdiocese archives.
- Pre-1837 marriage records are in the church registers, not the FamilySearch Parish Marriages collection (which begins 1837).
- Free-persons-of-color registers are physical at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Orleans Parish Civil District Court succession files older than what appears in FamilySearch collection 2078341 are physical at the courthouse or state archives.
- Tax rolls for the territorial and early statehood period are physical at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Newspaper microfilm for most titles remains physical at the New Orleans Public Library and LSU Libraries.

## Research tips
- **Start with notarial records.** Louisiana's civil-law system means that events documented in court records or deeds elsewhere were recorded as notarial acts in New Orleans. The NONARC is the single most important repository for 1800-1860 New Orleans research. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)), the notarial archives hold over 30 million pages from 1734 and survived the colonial fires.
- **Use Louisiana-specific terminology.** Search for 'successions' not 'probate', 'tutorship' not 'guardianship', and 'notarial acts' not 'deeds'. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)), these records are unique to Louisiana's civil-law tradition.
- **Treat fire-era absences as losses, not negatives.** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most colonial records. Missing records before ~1795 are almost certainly fire casualties. Church registers (1731+, with gaps) and the notarial archives are the best surviving sources for the period immediately before 1800 that bleeds into early-1800s family reconstruction.
- **Search across three languages.** Records in this period appear in French, Spanish, and English. A person's name may appear in three different forms across three record series. French and Spanish name equivalents should be searched alongside English forms.
- **Check St. Louis Cathedral registers before assuming no vital record.** Civil registration for births/marriages/deaths was not in place for most of this period; the Catholic church was the de facto civil registrar. FamilySearch collection 1612905 covers 1718-1925 and is the first stop.
- **The Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) is an index only.** It has 2,345,678 entries from 1819-1964 but zero attached images. Identifying a match requires ordering the underlying record from the Louisiana State Archives.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana pages returned generic content during this survey.** Re-run this guide or visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly (Louisiana Vital Records, Louisiana Church Records, Louisiana Probate Records, New Orleans Genealogy) before planning research around their absence from this guide.
