- **Port significance:** New Orleans was the second-busiest port of entry in the United States during 1800–1860, behind only New York. Passenger lists are a primary source for immigrant ancestors.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed in Orleans Parish courts, pre-1906 in any court of record); alien registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Orleans Parish Civil District Court or U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana (naturalizations).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. Examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed alongside parents.
- **Inland naturalization:** Declarations of intention could be filed in any court, so a person who arrived at New Orleans may have naturalized in a county or parish court far from the port.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Orleans Parish property tax and personal property tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Tax rolls survive from the territorial period (1803+).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; Louisiana Collection, Tulane University.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls can place a person in New Orleans in years between census enumerations and can document property ownership when deeds (notarial acts) are missing.

### Enslaved persons records
- **Types:** Manumission acts (notarial records at NONARC), succession inventories listing enslaved persons by name, bills of sale (notarial acts), baptismal records at St. Louis Cathedral (enslaved people were baptized), and separate registers of free people of color.
- **Free persons of color:** Louisiana maintained a legally distinct category of free people of color who were required to register; these registers survive at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Access:** NONARC for notarial acts; FamilySearch collection 1612905 for baptismal records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records + images); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (567,890 records + images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records + images); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 index entries, no images); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (004990115, 1803-1820, 167 images) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census collection (1810-1860 for Louisiana); passenger lists; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records, pension files, War of 1812 records | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Partial digitized runs of New Orleans newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans, Louisiana 1800–1820 (the query's internal end year was 1820, not 1860). For 1820–1860, no further digitized volumes were returned. The single volume is browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONARC) | 30+ million pages of notarial acts, 1734+ | In-person at 1340 Poydras St., New Orleans; partial index at notarialarchives.org |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records; Cabildo records; tax rolls; free-persons-of-color registers; Louisiana Statewide Death Index underlying records | In-person or mail request; some collections online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | St. Louis Cathedral registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, 1731+); other parish registers | In-person or written request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession (probate) files; guardianship (tutorship) records; court minutes | In-person |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Newspaper microfilm; city directories; local history collections | In-person |
| Tulane University, Louisiana Collection | Manuscript collections; plantation records; newspaper runs | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal court records including naturalization petitions; U.S. District Court Eastern Louisiana | In-person or NARA online access |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives (30+ million pages, 1734+) is not digitized or indexed online; only the single browse-only FamilySearch volume (004990115, 167 images, 1803-1820) exists digitally.
- St. Louis Cathedral registers beyond what is captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905 must be consulted through the Archdiocese archives.
- Pre-1837 marriage records are in the church registers, not the FamilySearch Parish Marriages collection (which begins 1837).
- Free-persons-of-color registers are physical at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Orleans Parish Civil District Court succession files older than what appears in FamilySearch collection 2078341 are physical at the courthouse or state archives.
- Tax rolls for the territorial and early statehood period are physical at the Louisiana State Archives.
- Newspaper microfilm for most titles remains physical at the New Orleans Public Library and LSU Libraries.

## Research tips
- **Start with notarial records.** Louisiana's civil-law system means that events documented in court records or deeds elsewhere were recorded as notarial acts in New Orleans. The NONARC is the single most important repository for 1800-1860 New Orleans research. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)), the notarial archives hold over 30 million pages from 1734 and survived the colonial fires.
- **Use Louisiana-specific terminology.** Search for 'successions' not 'probate', 'tutorship' not 'guardianship', and 'notarial acts' not 'deeds'. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)), these records are unique to Louisiana's civil-law tradition.
- **Treat fire-era absences as losses, not negatives.** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most colonial records. Missing records before ~1795 are almost certainly fire casualties. Church registers (1731+, with gaps) and the notarial archives are the best surviving sources for the period immediately before 1800 that bleeds into early-1800s family reconstruction.
- **Search across three languages.** Records in this period appear in French, Spanish, and English. A person's name may appear in three different forms across three record series. French and Spanish name equivalents should be searched alongside English forms.
- **Check St. Louis Cathedral registers before assuming no vital record.** Civil registration for births/marriages/deaths was not in place for most of this period; the Catholic church was the de facto civil registrar. FamilySearch collection 1612905 covers 1718-1925 and is the first stop.
- **The Statewide Death Index (collection 1543892) is an index only.** It has 2,345,678 entries from 1819-1964 but zero attached images. Identifying a match requires ordering the underlying record from the Louisiana State Archives.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana pages returned generic content during this survey.** Re-run this guide or visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly (Louisiana Vital Records, Louisiana Church Records, Louisiana Probate Records, New Orleans Genealogy) before planning research around their absence from this guide.

Here is what the locality-guide found for Boston in the 1840s:

---

The survey covers **Boston, Massachusetts in the 1840s**, the decade when tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants arrived through its port. Here are the key records and repositories:

### Port Arrival Records
- **Port of Boston customs passenger lists (1820–1891)** — originals held at the **National Archives at Boston in Waltham**; indexed on both **FamilySearch** (collection 1784312, over 1.2 million records) and **Ancestry**. One FamilySearch digitized volume (DGS 003345210, 389 images) specifically covers 1840–1850. Note: this volume is only 3% name-indexed but is **full-text searchable**, so keyword search works even without a complete name index.
- **Important caveat:** 1840s manifests recorded only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — they do *not* name the specific Irish county, parish, or townland.

### Bridging the Origin Gap
- **Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" database** (free, at infowanted.bc.edu, covering 1831–1921) — an invaluable resource for tracing Irish immigrants back to their home parishes.
- **Catholic church records** held by the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — baptismal and marriage registers frequently name the home parish in Ireland.

### Naturalization Records
- **FamilySearch collection 1459213** (345,678 naturalization records, 1790–1906) covers the period. Be aware that pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court (federal, state, or local), so all court levels in **Suffolk County** should be checked.

---

The recommended next step is to take specific names and arrival details and build a sequenced research plan across these record sets.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Settled 1630; city charter granted 1822
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston is the seat of Suffolk County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by tools for this query period; Wikipedia notes that by 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the Great Famine immigration wave
- **Economy:** Major seaport and manufacturing center; one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s
- **Ethnic composition:** Large and rapidly growing Irish immigrant population from mid-1840s onward; also English, German, and other European communities
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's and other Irish parishes from 1840s)
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest single wave of immigration in Boston's history; tens of thousands arrived through the Port of Boston in the 1840s

## Boundary changes
- Boston's city limits were largely stable during the 1840s–1860s; major annexations of surrounding towns (Roxbury 1868, Dorchester 1870, Charlestown and Brighton 1873, West Roxbury 1874) fall outside the target period
- Suffolk County was formed in 1643 as one of the original four Massachusetts counties; boundaries were stable throughout the target period

## Available record types

Note: The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts and Boston returned only generic content during this survey (see Research tips). All claims below come from wiki_search results, collections_search, volume_search, and Wikipedia.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts vital records returned only generic content during this survey; the specific year(s) for town-level and statewide registration could not be confirmed from tool results. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covers town-level births, marriages, and deaths well into the 1840s period — indexed and searchable by name at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (collection 2061550); Massachusetts State Archives; Boston City Archives
- **Gaps:** Newly arrived immigrants who died or married soon after arrival may appear only in church registers; consistency of civil recording improved through the period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; The Boston Pilot Missing Persons database

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's, and other Irish parishes); Congregationalist; Episcopal; Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Catholic confirmation registers
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives (Catholic records); FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657); individual church archives
- **Language:** English (Catholic registers for Irish immigrants generally in English or Latin)
- **Note:** Per wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston), the Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds Catholic parish registers documenting baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1840, 1850, and 1860 all fall within or immediately border the target period; the 1850 census was the first to name all household members (1840 names only the head of household)
- **State/provincial census:** Massachusetts did not hold a state census during this period
- **Other enumerations:** Federal mortality schedules (1850, 1860) record deaths in the year preceding the census
- **Access:** 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; 1840 is indexed by head of household only

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records) covers the target period
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Probate Court; FamilySearch collection 1678901 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Note:** Probate records for newly arrived immigrants are uncommon, but guardianship filings and intestate administrations may name family relationships

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New England system); Massachusetts is not a federal public-land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial-era grants; deeds held at the county level; the FamilySearch Wiki land and property page for Massachusetts could not be retrieved during this survey
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds, Boston; many deeds available online through the registry's own website

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War begins 1861 (just outside period)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized federal service records; Massachusetts State Archives for state-level records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Mount Auburn Cemetery (Cambridge, adjacent to Boston), Granary Burying Ground, Central Burying Ground; Holy Cross Cemetery and other Catholic cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) for major cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held at individual cemeteries or the Boston City Archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Boston Pilot (est. 1838, Irish Catholic newspaper); Boston Daily Atlas; Boston Advertiser
- **Where held:** Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" database, searchable free at infowanted.bc.edu (covers 1831-1921); historical Boston newspapers on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription)
- **Content value:** The Pilot's "Missing Persons" section — advertisements placed by Irish immigrants seeking relatives — is one of the most valuable 1840s Boston immigration resources and sometimes names the specific Irish parish of origin

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of Boston (primary); New York, Philadelphia, and Quebec are alternative ports some immigrants used before traveling to Boston
- **Record types:** Customs passenger lists 1820-1891 (NARA Record Group 36); naturalization records; alien registration (post-period)
- **Where held:** Originals at the National Archives at Boston (380 Trapelo Road, Waltham, MA); FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312, 1,234,567 records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312); also on Ancestry

- **Ethnic composition:** Large and rapidly growing Irish immigrant population from mid-1840s onward; also English, German, and other European communities
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopal, Methodist, Roman Catholic (Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's and other Irish parishes from 1840s)
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest single wave of immigration in Boston's history; tens of thousands arrived through the Port of Boston in the 1840s

## Boundary changes
- Boston's city limits were largely stable during the 1840s–1860s; major annexations of surrounding towns (Roxbury 1868, Dorchester 1870, Charlestown and Brighton 1873, West Roxbury 1874) fall outside the target period
- Suffolk County was formed in 1643 as one of the original four Massachusetts counties; boundaries were stable throughout the target period

Here is the locality guide for tracing Native American families in Oklahoma (Indian Territory) during the mid-1800s:

---

**Oklahoma / Indian Territory — Mid-1800s Locality Guide**

Oklahoma in the mid-1800s was **Indian Territory** — not yet a state (statehood came in 1907) — governed by the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole) under federal treaties and overseen by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. There was **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during this period.

### Key Record Types

- **Tribal Enrollment Rolls** — including the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852); these are the backbone of mid-1800s tribal genealogy
- **BIA Annuity Payment Rolls** — function as census substitutes, listing tribal members by household
- **Missionary Church Registers** — kept by Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions active from the 1820s onward
- **Dawes Rolls** — compiled in the late 1890s–early 1900s, but invaluable for working backward into earlier generations

### Key Collections on FamilySearch

| Collection | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 | 567,890 indexed records |
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 | 234,567 records |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 | 123,456 records |

One digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards (1840–1870) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

### Key Repositories

- **National Archives — Fort Worth, Texas**: Holds originals of Dawes Rolls, BIA agency files (Record Group 75), and Indian Territory federal court records
- **FamilySearch**: Digital access to indexed tribal rolls and church records
- **Oklahoma Historical Society**: Supplemental territorial and tribal records

### Critical Search Tips

1. **Always search under "Indian Territory," not "Oklahoma"** — no Oklahoma state records existed in this period, and county infrastructure did not exist at all.
2. **Civil War gap (1861–1865)**: The war created significant losses in church and agency records across Indian Territory. Bridge gaps using the earliest postwar BIA records and postwar tribal rolls.
3. **Tribe matters**: Different tribes maintained different records and dealt with different BIA agencies — identifying the specific tribe first narrows your search considerably.

### Recommended Next Step

Build a research plan targeting specific tribal rolls and BIA agency records for the particular ancestor and tribe you are tracing. If you share the tribe name and what you already know about the individual, I can help develop a targeted plan.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (Mid-1800s, ca. 1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status in target period:** Indian Territory (not yet a state; Oklahoma achieved statehood in 1907)
- **Authority:** Federal government via treaties; Bureau of Indian Affairs; tribal governments of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole)
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this jurisdiction and period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, cattle ranching; tribal economies disrupted by forced removal under the Indian Removal Act (1830)
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes, Osage, and other relocated nations; freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members) also present
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions active from the 1820s onward
- **Key historical events:** Indian Removal Act (1830), Trail of Tears (1830s–1840s), Civil War disruptions (1861–1865)

## Boundary changes
- In the mid-1800s the area was designated Indian Territory — set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for relocated Native American nations. It was not a state or organized territory with county government.
- Oklahoma Territory was organized separately in 1890 from unassigned lands.
- Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory merged to form the State of Oklahoma in 1907.
- Pre-statehood records are held and indexed under 'Indian Territory' designations at the National Archives. Searching under 'Oklahoma' alone will miss the mid-1800s records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No state civil registration existed during the target period. Indian Territory had no civil registration mechanism.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death registration for 1840–1880.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls record family groupings; BIA annuity payment rolls name individuals and households; missionary church registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials.

### Church / missionary records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward, per [Oklahoma Native American Records — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, school enrollment lists, community membership, baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection ID 1654321; 123,456 records, 61,728 images) covers this period. Originals at denominational archives and the National Archives.
- **Language:** English.

### Census / tribal enrollment records
- **Federal census:** Indian Territory was not systematically included in standard federal decennial censuses during the mid-1800s.
- **Tribal rolls — primary source:** The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) are key mid-century rolls. Per [Oklahoma Native American Records — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls), the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the most widely used enrollment records and record name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation; work backward from them to the earlier rolls.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (collection ID 1987432; 567,890 records, 283,945 images) — indexed + images.
- **Digitized volume:** 1 volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870, 940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable (image group 002298871) — indexed + images.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts administered probate and civil matters for tribal members. Federal courts in Indian Territory handled some cases.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Fort Worth, TX holds Indian Territory federal court records. Individual tribal archives hold tribal court records.

### Land records
- **System:** Prior to the Dawes Act (1887), land was held communally by each tribe. Federal and tribal governments issued land-related documents through treaties.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection ID 1541872; 234,567 records, 117,283 images) covers the target period — indexed + images.
- **Where held:** National Archives; Bureau of Land Management GLO records for post-allotment patents; tribal archives for communal land records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — members of all Five Civilized Tribes served on both Union and Confederate sides.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants. Confederate and Union Indian unit records held at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives; Fold3.com indexes many military records online.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com and BillionGraves cover many Oklahoma/Indian Territory cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Mission and church cemeteries maintained burial registers; some tribal cemeteries have separately maintained records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Phoenix (1828–1835) is an early example; tribal newspapers were published in Indian Territory. Newspapers.com has some historical Oklahoma coverage.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land notices, tribal council proceedings.

### Immigration / removal records
- **Relevant context:** Removal-era records document forced migration of tribes from the southeastern U.S. to Indian Territory in the 1830s–1840s. These records name individuals and families and are essential for tracing ancestors before they appear in Indian Territory.
- **Record types:** Removal rolls, treaty records, emigration records.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C. and Fort Worth, TX.
- **Content note:** Removal rolls and annuity lists enumerate every household member — examine the full entry for all family members, including children.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tribal nations levied taxes within their jurisdictions. BIA annuity payment rolls functionally document tribal members across census-equivalent periods.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs).

### BIA agency records (other)
- The Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained annuity payment rolls, correspondence, school records, and agency files for Indian Territory agencies — these are the closest equivalent to vital and civil records for this period and population.
- Per [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records), these are now held at the National Archives.
- Some series are indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; many boxes remain browse-only or physical-only.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (123,456 records); 1 digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; U.S. Federal Census collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files for Indian Territory units | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | BIA Record Group 75; Indian Territory federal court records; Dawes Rolls originals at Fort Worth, TX facility | Free to request; in-person or digital access |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including tribal publications | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching Indian Territory, 1840–1870 (totalResults: 1). The FamilySearch collections survey returned 3 collections overlapping the 1840–1880 target period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives, Fort Worth, TX | Dawes Rolls, BIA agency records (RG 75), Indian Territory federal court records | In-person; some digitized online |
| National Archives, Washington, D.C. | Treaty records, removal rolls, NARA RG 75 correspondence | In-person; archival request |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | State and territorial records, newspapers, local histories | In-person / OHS online portal |
| Tribal nation archives (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) | Tribal court records, tribal census rolls, council minutes | Contact individual tribe's THPO |
| Denominational archives | Missionary registers | Contact denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Tribal court records held at individual tribal archives are largely not digitized.
- BIA correspondence and agency-level records in NARA RG 75 are partially digitized; many boxes remain browse-only or physical-only.
- Early removal-era records (1830s) at NARA are not fully indexed or digitized.
- Tribal nation internal archives (council minutes, tribal court dockets) are not on any public online platform.

## Known record losses
- The Civil War (1861–1865) caused significant destruction of Indian Territory records — agency records, church registers, and tribal documents were lost or disrupted. Bridge the gap using the earliest postwar BIA records and postwar tribal rolls.

## Research tips
- Work backward from the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) — the most widely used Five Civilized Tribes enrollment records, indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry — to earlier mid-century rolls such as the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852). Source: [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- BIA annuity payment rolls are the functional equivalent of census records for the mid-1800s in Indian Territory: they list tribal members receiving annual treaty payments by household.
- Missionary records (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) name converts, students, and community members and often supply family relationships not found elsewhere. Source: [Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- Search records under 'Indian Territory,' not 'Oklahoma' — the area had no state or county structure during 1840–1880, and most databases are indexed under the territorial designation.
- Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own government and archives; contact the tribal historic preservation office (THPO) directly for records outside what NARA holds — especially tribal court records and council minutes.
- A negative online result is not absence: many BIA and tribal records remain undigitized; in-person research at NARA Fort Worth or tribal archives is often required.

output.text_response:
Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Pennsylvania in the late 1700s had no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths — that system did not begin at the state level until 1906. For Quaker ancestors, this means the Society of Friends' own meeting records are not a supplement to vital records; **they are the vital records.** Monthly meetings kept birth registers, death and burial books, marriage records (with a certificate signed by every witness present, sometimes a hundred people), disownment proceedings, and Certificates of Removal when a member moved to a new meeting.

**Key geographic context:** The densest Quaker populations were in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties.

---

### Primary Repositories

**Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College**
The single most important repository for pre-1800 Pennsylvania meeting registers. Holds original registers from most Pennsylvania monthly meetings.

**Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College**
The companion repository to Swarthmore; the two institutions split holdings and together hold the bulk of surviving Pennsylvania Quaker records.

**FamilySearch microfilm**
Many meeting registers have been filmed. Note: FamilySearch's digitized holdings for this period are thin — the survey confirmed only one browse-only volume (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 145 images, not name-indexed). Most Quaker records require ordering microfilm or visiting Swarthmore/Haverford directly.

---

### Record Types to Seek

| Record Type | What It Contains |
|---|---|
| **Birth registers** | Name, birth date, parents — the Quaker equivalent of a baptismal record |
| **Death & burial books** | Date of death and burial; sometimes age and surviving relatives |
| **Marriage records** | Full marriage certificate signed by every witness present (often 50–100 signatures), making these especially valuable for identifying the extended community |
| **Certificates of Removal** | Issued when a member moved to another meeting — functionally an emigration record, tracking families across county and state lines |
| **Disownment proceedings** | Formal records of members separated from the meeting; *particularly valuable for 1775–1783*, when many were disowned for bearing arms in the Revolution |

---

### Finding Aid: Hinshaw's Encyclopedia

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** — abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and is the fastest entry point before requesting microfilm. Available at many genealogical libraries and through interlibrary loan.

---

### Next Steps

To narrow the search, identify which **specific monthly meeting** your family belonged to (the township or county is usually enough), then locate that meeting's registers at Swarthmore, Haverford, or on FamilySearch microfilm. If you can share what you know about the county or township, the search can be focused considerably.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Province of Pennsylvania established 1681 by William Penn as a Quaker haven. Became the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 1787 on ratification of the U.S. Constitution.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early state capital); Lancaster served briefly as state capital during the Revolution.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony) until 1776; independent Commonwealth thereafter.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools. Quaker communities were concentrated especially in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties per Wikipedia.
- **Economy:** Mixed farming, milling, and Philadelphia trade. Quaker merchants and craftsmen predominated in Philadelphia.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers were the founding group; German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite) spread across the interior by mid-century; Scots-Irish Presbyterians filled the backcountry.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) affected western counties; Revolutionary War (1775–1783) caused mass Quaker disownments for military service; post-war migration westward and southward documented in removal certificates.

## Boundary changes
- The Province of Pennsylvania existed from 1681 to 1787. No internal boundary split affects where records are held at the state level, but county formation was ongoing: new counties were carved from older ones throughout the 1750–1800 period. Always identify which county a township belonged to at the date of a specific event — the county court (not the township) held civil records, while the Quaker meeting held its own records independently of county lines.
- The late 1700s straddles two jurisdictional eras: colonial (pre-1787, records generated under the Penn proprietary) and early statehood (1787 onward). Land records in particular reflect this split — see Land Records section.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** (state level). No civil registration existed in the late 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for 1750–1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting registers are the primary substitute for vital records throughout this period. They recorded births, marriages, and deaths with substantially more detail than most later civil certificates. Other denominations (Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian) kept separate parish registers.

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends) — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD
- **Meeting structure:** Three levels — Monthly Meeting (local congregation, the primary record-keeping unit), Quarterly Meeting (regional, several monthly meetings), Yearly Meeting (governing body for Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and New York: the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting).
- **Record types recorded at the Monthly Meeting level:**
  - Birth registrations (entered by parents, often retrospectively)
  - Death and burial records
  - Marriage records — uniquely, Quaker marriages were self-performed before the assembled meeting, and the marriage certificate was signed by every person present (commonly 50–100 witnesses); this makes it a community membership snapshot
  - Disownments and disciplinary proceedings — significant spike during the Revolutionary War (1775–1783) when members who bore arms were disowned
  - Certificates of Removal — issued when a member transferred to a new monthly meeting; essential for tracking migration
  - Meeting minutes at all three levels
- **Where held:**
  - **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA): the largest single repository of American Quaker records (confirmed by Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).
  - **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA): major collection, particularly strong for Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records (confirmed by Wikipedia).
  - **FamilySearch:** has microfilmed many monthly meeting registers and minutes. The survey found 1 digitized volume for 1750–1800 through the FamilySearch volume search: DGS 001188322, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 145 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes), abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states — confirmed as a key finding aid by the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts. This is the first resource to check before going to original registers.
- **Digitization level:** One browse-only FamilySearch volume confirmed (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting). Most monthly meeting registers are microfilm at the FamilySearch Library or physical at Swarthmore/Haverford.

### Church records — Other denominations
- **Denominations present:** German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Denominational archives, state historical societies, and FamilySearch microfilm. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) holds many colonial-era church registers.
- **Language:** German Lutheran and German Reformed records are commonly in German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering Pennsylvania is **1790**. It is a heads-of-household enumeration — it names the household head only, with tallies for free white males, free white females, and enslaved persons. No census covers 1750–1789.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no territorial or state census during this period.
- **Substitute enumerations:** County tax lists (ratables) are the primary substitute for the pre-1790 census. They enumerate taxable persons by township, documenting presence year by year. Pennsylvania Archives (the published series) reprints many colonial and early state tax lists.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Pennsylvania is fully indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), inventories, guardianships.
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania probate records at FamilySearch go back to 1683. The collection Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) covers this period; it contains 3.2 million images but is **browse-only** (0 indexed records). Probate was handled at the county level.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills offices (originals); Pennsylvania State Archives; FamilySearch (browse-only images).
- **Research value:** Wills from this period frequently name all children, including married daughters under their married names, and grandchildren — making them a primary source for family reconstruction when meeting records are incomplete.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Before 1776, the Penn Proprietors issued warrants and grants. After 1776, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania took over land distribution through the General Land Office (now the Pennsylvania State Archives).
- **Types:** Warrant registers, survey books, patents, deeds at county Recorder of Deeds.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives holds the warrant registers and survey books. County Recorder of Deeds offices hold deed books. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Pennsylvania Land and Property during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly.
- **Quaker relevance:** Quaker families frequently appear in proprietary land grants; the Penn family and many grantees were Friends.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Critical Quaker note:** Many Quakers were disowned during the Revolutionary War for bearing arms. The disownment records at the monthly meeting level are the record of this. Quakers who served in the militia or Continental Army will NOT typically appear in military pension files under their Quaker identity after disownment — check both the meeting records AND the pension files.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (Fold3 and Ancestry have digitized collections). Pennsylvania Archives (published series, 138 volumes) includes muster rolls, militia records, and pension records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC), Pennsylvania State Archives, Fold3 (online, subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Quakers buried in plain, often unmarked graves in meeting burial grounds — grave markers were considered worldly vanity until the mid-19th century. Do not expect tombstone inscriptions; rely on meeting burial registers instead.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave covers some Friends burial grounds; coverage for the 1750–1800 period is thin.
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers, held at Swarthmore and Haverford and on FamilySearch microfilm.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, founded 1728) is the principal colonial and early national newspaper. It ran legal notices, runaway-servant ads, and occasional vital notices.
- **Where held:** Digitized at Accessible Archives and partially through other services. Physical microfilm at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and many libraries.
- **Content value for this period:** Legal notices and property sales are more common than family vital notices for Friends.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania-bound Quaker immigrants from England, Wales, and Ireland.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (ship manifests) for arrivals at Philadelphia, naturalization records (for non-British immigrants).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania colonial-era arrivals are in published lists (Strassburger & Hinke for Germans; Quaker arrivals documented in meeting transfer certificates). NARA holds federal records after 1820. The FamilySearch collection Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957) overlaps this period.
- **Certificates of removal as migration records:** Within the Quaker system, every cross-meeting move generated a Certificate of Removal — functionally an internal emigration record documenting origin meeting, destination meeting, and character endorsement.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County assessment lists (taxables), listing land, livestock, and occupations by township.
- **Date range:** Surviving lists go back to the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Pennsylvania Archives (published series) reprints many lists. County historical societies hold originals.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary census substitute for 1750–1789, before the first federal census.

### Other record types
- **Quaker school records:** Monthly meetings ran schools; attendance and enrollment records survive in some meeting archives at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Sufferings records:** Meetings recorded members who suffered losses (property seizures, fines) for refusal to pay war taxes or perform militia duty during the Revolution — a unique Quaker record class.
- **Meeting membership lists:** Some meetings compiled formal membership rolls; check the archive for each meeting.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, browse-only, 145 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 and later); Fold3 military records; Pennsylvania archives series | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military records | Free (some digitized) |
| FindAGrave | Some Friends burial grounds (thin pre-1800 coverage) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 across all record types. This is a very sparse digitized set for this place and period — most Quaker meeting registers are microfilm at the FamilySearch Library or physical at Swarthmore College and Haverford College.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore PA | Largest U.S. Quaker records collection: monthly meeting registers, minutes, removal certificates, sufferings records | In-person (appointments recommended); some finding aids online at swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College, Haverford PA | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and related collections | In-person; online catalog at triptych.brynmawr.edu |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia PA | Colonial church registers, colonial newspapers, land records, published Pennsylvania Archives | In-person; some digitized at HSP's DigitalLibrary |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg PA | Land warrant registers, survey books, colonial and state government records, tax lists | In-person and online request |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City UT | Microfilm of monthly meeting registers for many PA meetings | Free on-site; some digitized online |

## Records NOT online
- Most Pennsylvania Quaker monthly meeting birth, marriage, death, and removal registers for 1750–1800 are NOT online in searchable form. # Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Province of Pennsylvania established 1681 by William Penn as a Quaker haven. Became the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania in 1787 on ratification of the U.S. Constitution.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early state capital); Lancaster served briefly as state capital during the Revolution.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colony) until 1776; independent Commonwealth thereafter.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools. Quaker communities were concentrated especially in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties per Wikipedia.
- **Economy:** Mixed farming, milling, and Philadelphia trade. Quaker merchants and craftsmen predominated in Philadelphia.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers were the founding group; German settlers (Lutheran, Reformed, Mennonite) spread across the interior by mid-century; Scots-Irish Presbyterians filled the backcountry.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763) affected western counties; Revolutionary War (1775–1783) caused mass Quaker disownments for military service; post-war migration westward and southward documented in removal certificates.

## Boundary changes
- The Province of Pennsylvania existed from 1681 to 1787. No internal boundary split affects where records are held at the state level, but county formation was ongoing: new counties were carved from older ones throughout the 1750–1800 period. Always identify which county a township belonged to at the date of a specific event — the county court (not the township) held civil records, while the Quaker meeting held its own records independently of county lines.
- The late 1700s straddles two jurisdictional eras: colonial (pre-1787, records generated under the Penn proprietary) and early statehood (1787 onward). Land records in particular reflect this split — see Land Records section.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** (state level). No civil registration existed in the late 1700s.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for 1750–1800.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting registers are the primary substitute for vital records throughout this period. They recorded births, marriages, and deaths with substantially more detail than most later civil certificates. Other denominations (Lutheran, Reformed, Presbyterian) kept separate parish registers.

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends) — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD
- **Meeting structure:** Three levels — Monthly Meeting (local congregation, the primary record-keeping unit), Quarterly Meeting (regional, several monthly meetings), Yearly Meeting (governing body for Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and New York: the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting).
- **Record types recorded at the Monthly Meeting level:**
  - Birth registrations (entered by parents, often retrospectively)
  - Death and burial records
  - Marriage records — uniquely, Quaker marriages were self-performed before the assembled meeting, and the marriage certificate was signed by every person present (commonly 50–100 witnesses); this makes it a community membership snapshot
  - Disownments and disciplinary proceedings — significant spike during the Revolutionary War (1775–1783) when members who bore arms were disowned
  - Certificates of Removal — issued when a member transferred to a new monthly meeting; essential for tracking migration
  - Meeting minutes at all three levels
- **Where held:**
  - **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA): the largest single repository of American Quaker records (confirmed by Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania).
  - **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA): major collection, particularly strong for Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records (confirmed by Wikipedia).
  - **FamilySearch:** has microfilmed many monthly meeting registers and minutes. The survey found 1 digitized volume for 1750–1800 through the FamilySearch volume search: DGS 001188322, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 145 images, **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes), abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states — confirmed as a key finding aid by the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts. This is the first resource to check before going to original registers.
- **Digitization level:** One browse-only FamilySearch volume confirmed (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting). Most monthly meeting registers are microfilm at the FamilySearch Library or physical at Swarthmore/Haverford.

### Church records — Other denominations
- **Denominations present:** German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, Mennonite, Moravian.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Denominational archives, state historical societies, and FamilySearch microfilm. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) holds many colonial-era church registers.
- **Language:** German Lutheran and German Reformed records are commonly in German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census covering Pennsylvania is **1790**. It is a heads-of-household enumeration — it names the household head only, with tallies for free white males, free white females, and enslaved persons. No census covers 1750–1789.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no territorial or state census during this period.
- **Substitute enumerations:** County tax lists (ratables) are the primary substitute for the pre-1790 census. They enumerate taxable persons by township, documenting presence year by year. Pennsylvania Archives (the published series) reprints many colonial and early state tax lists.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census for Pennsylvania is fully indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), inventories, guardianships.
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania probate records at FamilySearch go back to 1683. The collection Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) covers this period; it contains 3.2 million images but is **browse-only** (0 indexed records). Probate was handled at the county level.
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills offices (originals); Pennsylvania State Archives; FamilySearch (browse-only images).
- **Research value:** Wills from this period frequently name all children, including married daughters under their married names, and grandchildren — making them a primary source for family reconstruction when meeting records are incomplete.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Before 1776, the Penn Proprietors issued warrants and grants. After 1776, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania took over land distribution through the General Land Office (now the Pennsylvania State Archives).
- **Types:** Warrant registers, survey books, patents, deeds at county Recorder of Deeds.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives holds the warrant registers and survey books. County Recorder of Deeds offices hold deed books. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for Pennsylvania Land and Property during this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property directly.
- **Quaker relevance:** Quaker families frequently appear in proprietary land grants; the Penn family and many grantees were Friends.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Critical Quaker note:** Many Quakers were disowned during the Revolutionary War for bearing arms. The disownment records at the monthly meeting level are the record of this. Quakers who served in the militia or Continental Army will NOT typically appear in military pension files under their Quaker identity after disownment — check both the meeting records AND the pension files.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (Fold3 and Ancestry have digitized collections). Pennsylvania Archives (published series, 138 volumes) includes muster rolls, militia records, and pension records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington DC), Pennsylvania State Archives, Fold3 (online, subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Quakers buried in plain, often unmarked graves in meeting burial grounds — grave markers were considered worldly vanity until the mid-19th century. Do not expect tombstone inscriptions; rely on meeting burial registers instead.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave covers some Friends burial grounds; coverage for the 1750–1800 period is thin.
- **Physical records:** Meeting burial registers, held at Swarthmore and Haverford and on FamilySearch microfilm.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, founded 1728) is the principal colonial and early national newspaper. It ran legal notices, runaway-servant ads, and occasional vital notices.
- **Where held:** Digitized at Accessible Archives and partially through other services. Physical microfilm at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and many libraries.
- **Content value for this period:** Legal notices and property sales are more common than family vital notices for Friends.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for Pennsylvania-bound Quaker immigrants from England, Wales, and Ireland.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (ship manifests) for arrivals at Philadelphia, naturalization records (for non-British immigrants).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania colonial-era arrivals are in published lists (Strassburger & Hinke for Germans; Quaker arrivals documented in meeting transfer certificates). NARA holds federal records after 1820. The FamilySearch collection Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957) overlaps this period.
- **Certificates of removal as migration records:** Within the Quaker system, every cross-meeting move generated a Certificate of Removal — functionally an internal emigration record documenting origin meeting, destination meeting, and character endorsement.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County assessment lists (taxables), listing land, livestock, and occupations by township.
- **Date range:** Surviving lists go back to the colonial period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Pennsylvania Archives (published series) reprints many lists. County historical societies hold originals.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary census substitute for 1750–1789, before the first federal census.

### Other record types
- **Quaker school records:** Monthly meetings ran schools; attendance and enrollment records survive in some meeting archives at Swarthmore and Haverford.
- **Sufferings records:** Meetings recorded members who suffered losses (property seizures, fines) for refusal to pay war taxes or perform militia duty during the Revolution — a unique Quaker record class.
- **Meeting membership lists:** Some meetings compiled formal membership rolls; check the archive for each meeting.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (DGS 001188322, browse-only, 145 images); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 and later); Fold3 military records; Pennsylvania archives series | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records, passenger lists, military records | Free (some digitized) |
| FindAGrave | Some Friends burial grounds (thin pre-1800 coverage) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume search returned 1 digitized volume for Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 across all record types. This is a very sparse digitized set for this place and period — most Quaker meeting registers are microfilm at the FamilySearch Library or physical at Swarthmore College and Haverford College.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population figures did not resolve from available tools. Per Wikipedia, Pittsburgh became the center of America's steel industry in the late 1800s and was one of the fastest-growing industrial cities of the era.
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing (Carnegie Steel and other firms), iron, coke, and glass production — the dominant industries directly shape which occupational records survive.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant workers, per Wikipedia; each group clustered in distinct neighborhoods and parishes.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (multiple national parishes serving specific ethnic communities — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), Presbyterian, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Key historical events:** Carnegie Steel's expansion 1870s–1890s; Homestead Strike 1892 (generating labor and court records); major immigration waves 1880s–1900s.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County formed 1788 — records predating county formation are in Washington and Westmoreland counties.
- The independent City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was a separate municipality through the entire target period, not annexed until 1907. Families living in Allegheny City during 1870–1900 have records filed under that city, not Pittsburgh.
- County boundaries were otherwise stable through the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; consult [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) directly for registration start dates by level. The FamilySearch collection Pennsylvania Death Certificates (id: 2255317) begins in 1906, indicating statewide death registration started that year — outside the main target period.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania had no statewide birth or death registration during 1870–1900. County-level marriage registration existed; FamilySearch holds Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 indexed records) and Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records). Church records are the primary vital source for births and deaths in this period.
- **Gaps:** Birth and death civil records are largely absent for 1870–1900; statewide death certificates exist only from 1906. Pre-registration: use ethnic church registers, city directories, and newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)), Catholic ethnic parishes each served a specific national community — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish. German Lutheran and Reformed congregations served older German-immigrant families.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; Catholic baptism registers often record parents' village of origin in Europe — a key link for tracing back to the home country.
- **Where held:** Individual parish archives; Diocese of Pittsburgh archives; FamilySearch Catalog (search for Allegheny County microfilm). Records in Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian are in the community's language, not English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses survive for Pittsburgh. The 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921 — a critical gap at the height of the steel boom.
- **Occupation listings:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)), federal census schedules 1870–1900 list each person's occupation — entries such as "puddler," "roller," "heater," or "laborer" tie a person directly to the steel industry.
- **Access:** Federal census records are name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; 1880 and 1900 also list parents' birthplaces, pointing back to the country of origin.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; FamilySearch holds Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (id: 1999196, over 3.2 million images) — browse-only with no name index; must be browsed image by image.
- **Court records:** Naturalization records before 1906 could be filed in any Pennsylvania court — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, U.S. Circuit Court, or U.S. District Court. FamilySearch holds Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (volume 008120443, 351 images, 15% name-indexed); unindexed images must be browsed.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (Register of Wills, Prothonotary); National Archives at Philadelphia (RG 21 for federal court naturalization records), per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania uses metes-and-bounds surveying based on the original Penn proprietorship grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; consult [Pennsylvania Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property) directly.
- **Types and access:** Deeds, mortgages, and property tax records held at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds. In a dense urban industrial area, most workers rented rather than owned, so land records are less central than in rural settings but tax records still locate individuals annually.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) predates the period but many steelworkers were veterans; Spanish-American War (1898) falls at the period's end.
- **Record types:** Civil War pension files are especially valuable — they contain family affidavits, correspondence, and widow's claims with detailed personal information. Service and pension records are on FamilySearch and Fold3 (fold3.com).
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Pennsylvania State Archives (state militia and National Guard records).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) provides searchable grave records for many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries, including ethnic Catholic cemeteries that served specific national communities.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are held by individual cemeteries or the administering church; some are held by local historical societies.
- **Note:** Ethnic Catholic cemeteries often served a single national community and were administered by the parish — tracing the cemetery follows tracing the parish.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh had multiple daily newspapers in this period including the Pittsburgh Gazette and Pittsburgh Post; Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) has historical Pittsburgh newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries may give birthplace, survivors, and employer; marriage notices name families; coverage of the 1892 Homestead Strike names individual workers. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh maintains newspaper collections.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most eastern European and Italian immigrants arrived through New York (Ellis Island and Castle Garden); Irish and earlier German immigrants often through Baltimore or Philadelphia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, declarations of intention ("first papers"), petitions for naturalization, and certificate applications — all generated in Allegheny County even when arrival was at a distant port. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)), naturalization records are at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Post-1906 naturalization petitions include the applicant's birthplace, physical description, spouse's name, and arrival details — examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property and personal property assessments; annual records from 1788 onward.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can locate a person between census years and partially replace the missing 1890 census. Held at Allegheny County and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Other record types: Industrial and occupational records
*This record class is the primary focus of this survey.*
- **Company records:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)), company employment records are fragmentary — some survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives**. Contact both repositories directly; holdings are not fully catalogued online.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s; per the FamilySearch Wiki, directories list each resident's occupation, employer, and street address. Some Pittsburgh directories are also on Ancestry and the Internet Archive.
- **Union and state records:** Union membership lists (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers) are at Rivers of Steel archives and University of Pittsburgh labor collections. Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspector reports listing workers by establishment, per the FamilySearch Wiki — held at Pennsylvania State Archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765); Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900 (indexed); passenger lists; city directories | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Naturalization records, federal court records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania level (complete set — no further pages). These are: Probate Records 1683–1994 (1,180 images, browse-only), Death Records 1852–1968 (674 images, browse-only), and Naturalization Records 1790–1915 (351 images, 15% name-indexed). Neither volume_search nor collections_search returned Allegheny County-specific indexed collections — search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for Allegheny County microfilm, which may not be surfaced by these tools.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Industrial/immigration records; fragmentary company employment records | In-person; contact for access |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area | Steel company and union records | In-person; contact for access |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1810s; local history collection | In-person; some materials online |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Naturalization petitions; deeds; probate; court records | In-person |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Naturalization records (RG 21); federal court records | In-person / online request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Militia records; tax records; factory inspector reports | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish register copies | Contact diocese |

## Records NOT online

- **Company employment records:** Steel company personnel files are fragmentary and largely not published online; those that survive are at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives.
- **Pre-1906 birth and death records:** No statewide civil registration existed; coverage is incomplete and mostly not online.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization records (bulk unindexed):** FamilySearch volume 008120443 is only 15% indexed; most must be browsed or requested from the National Archives at Philadelphia.
- **Catholic ethnic parish registers:** Most remain at the parish or diocesan archives with limited online presence.
- **Union membership records:** Not digitized or available online for this period.
- **Pennsylvania factory inspector reports:** Paper records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not available online.

## Known record losses

- **1890 federal census:** Largely destroyed by a 1921 Washington, D.C. fire — a critical gap for Pittsburgh families at the height of the steel boom. Bridge with tax lists, city directories, and 1880/1900 census.
- **Corporate employment records:** Many steel company employment records were discarded during corporate consolidations or failures; surviving fragments at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are not comprehensive.

## Research tips
- **Start with city directories, not vital records.** For 1870–1900 Pittsburgh, statewide civil registration did not exist; the city directory is often the first document to place a person, name their occupation and employer, and give a street address. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh directories from the 1810s, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **Identify the ethnic parish.** Catholic church records are the primary vital record for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and Irish families. Each national community had its own parish, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)); baptism registers often record the parents' village of origin, providing a direct line back to Europe.
- **Check naturalization records early.** Declarations of intention and petitions filed at the Allegheny County courthouse or federal courts frequently include native village, occupation, and (post-1906) spouse's name. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790–1915 is only 15% indexed — also search the National Archives at Philadelphia (RG 21), per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **Use federal census occupation fields.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 census schedules list occupation; 1880 and 1900 also list parents' birthplaces. These link a person to the steel industry and point back to the country of origin.
- **Contact the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel directly.** Company employment records for Pittsburgh steel mills are fragmentary and not catalogued online; both hold surviving records, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **Search Allegheny City separately.** The independent City of Allegheny was a distinct municipality until 1907; families living there have records filed separately from Pittsburgh. Search both when a family's address is unclear.
