| National Archives at Philadelphia | Naturalization records (RG 21); federal court records | In-person / online request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Militia records; tax records; factory inspector reports | In-person / online request |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish register copies | Contact diocese |

## Records NOT online

- **Company employment records:** Steel company personnel files are fragmentary and largely not published online; those that survive are at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives.
- **Pre-1906 birth and death records:** No statewide civil registration existed; coverage is incomplete and mostly not online.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization records (bulk unindexed):** FamilySearch volume 008120443 is only 15% indexed; most must be browsed or requested from the National Archives at Philadelphia.
- **Catholic ethnic parish registers:** Most remain at the parish or diocesan archives with limited online presence.
- **Union membership records:** Not digitized or available online for this period.
- **Pennsylvania factory inspector reports:** Paper records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; not available online.

## Known record losses

- **1890 federal census:** Largely destroyed by a 1921 Washington, D.C. fire — a critical gap for Pittsburgh families at the height of the steel boom. Bridge with tax lists, city directories, and 1880/1900 census.
- **Corporate employment records:** Many steel company employment records were discarded during corporate consolidations or failures; surviving fragments at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel are not comprehensive.

## Research tips
- **Start with city directories, not vital records.** For 1870–1900 Pittsburgh, statewide civil registration did not exist; the city directory is often the first document to place a person, name their occupation and employer, and give a street address. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh directories from the 1810s, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **Identify the ethnic parish.** Catholic church records are the primary vital record for Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, and Irish families. Each national community had its own parish, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)); baptism registers often record the parents' village of origin, providing a direct line back to Europe.
- **Check naturalization records early.** Declarations of intention and petitions filed at the Allegheny County courthouse or federal courts frequently include native village, occupation, and (post-1906) spouse's name. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790–1915 is only 15% indexed — also search the National Archives at Philadelphia (RG 21), per the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **Use federal census occupation fields.** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 census schedules list occupation; 1880 and 1900 also list parents' birthplaces. These link a person to the steel industry and point back to the country of origin.
- **Contact the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel directly.** Company employment records for Pittsburgh steel mills are fragmentary and not catalogued online; both hold surviving records, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)).
- **Search Allegheny City separately.** The independent City of Allegheny was a distinct municipality until 1907; families living there have records filed separately from Pittsburgh. Search both when a family's address is unclear.

**Philadelphia County, 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Records & Repositories**

Philadelphia County in the 1780–1810 period had **no civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths — Pennsylvania did not require statewide vital registration until 1906. Key sources for tracing families affected by the epidemic:

### Epidemic-Specific Records
- **Mathew Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793)** — lists names of the dead; held by the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**. This is the single most important epidemic resource.
- **Bush Hill Hospital records** — manuscript records of the makeshift epidemic hospital
- **Minutes of the citizen Committee** — the volunteer committee that organized relief efforts during the outbreak
- These are largely unindexed and require in-person or correspondence visits.

### Church Records (Primary Source for Deaths & Burials)
Because there was no civil registration, **church burial registers** are the main death record:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal)
- **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'** (Swedish Lutheran)
- Other Philadelphia congregations also kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers

### FamilySearch Online Collections
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** — 3.2 million browse-only images; estate filings from 1793–1795 are a high-priority target for epidemic deaths
- Pennsylvania marriage collections covering the period
- **1790 and 1800 federal censuses**
- **1798 Federal Direct Tax** (a substitute for a census year)
- **Philadelphia city directories** from 1785 onward

### Key Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Carey's account, church records, family papers |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Committee minutes, municipal records |
| FamilySearch.org | Probate, census, marriage records |

### Migration Caveat
Thousands **fled the city** during the epidemic. Families may appear in records from neighboring counties — **Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, or Chester Counties (PA)** — or across the Delaware River in **New Jersey**. Check those jurisdictions as well.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, Yellow Fever Epidemic 1793)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682; city incorporated 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** City of Philadelphia (coextensive with the county for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in 1793 (Wikipedia, Yellow fever epidemic of 1793). No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Major seaport and U.S. capital (1790–1800); trade, shipping, crafts, and finance dominated
- **Ethnic composition:** English, German, Irish, Scots-Irish, Dutch, African American; prominent Quaker community; sustained immigrant arrivals via the Port of Philadelphia
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers, Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Roman Catholic, Methodist
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents (roughly one-tenth of the population); thousands fled the city. Philadelphia was the U.S. capital 1790–1800.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was formed in 1682 and remained geographically stable throughout the 1780–1810 period. The city and county were not formally consolidated until 1854. For this period, city and county records exist as distinct series but cover the same territory.
- No boundary changes affected the county during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide vital registration until 1906 (state level). No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1793. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1793. Church registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the sole primary vital-record source for all events in this period.
- **Where held:** Individual denominational archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (which has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records)
- **Gaps:** Rapid epidemic deaths in August–November 1793 may have outpaced church registration capacity; some burials may be undocumented in any church register.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; Committee appointed by citizens records; Bush Hill hospital records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Roman Catholic, Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; individual church archives; FamilySearch microfilm. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Yellow-fever-specific sources:** The FamilySearch Wiki specifically names burial records from Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as key sources for epidemic deaths. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))
- **Digitization:** 1 digitized volume on FamilySearch — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322), 145 images. Browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Must be navigated image by image.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (taken August 1790, three years before the epidemic) and the 1800 federal census are the two enumerations bracketing the event. Both are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania county tax lists serve as intercensal substitutes. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax enumerated every household, real property, and personal property in Philadelphia — a critical substitute record that falls between the 1790 and 1800 censuses.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed online (FamilySearch, Ancestry). The 1798 Federal Direct Tax is available on Ancestry.com.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, estate inventories, petitions; Orphans' Court guardianship cases (expected to have surged in 1793–1794 as epidemic orphans were placed)
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records from 1682 onward
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196) holds 3,200,560 images, browse-only (0 indexed records — must be navigated by date and ward). Also held at the Philadelphia Register of Wills and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Research priority:** Estate filings from late 1793 through 1795 document survivors, heirs, and family relationships for the approximately 5,000 epidemic dead — a high-priority source when vital records are absent.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is an original colony/state, not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office issued warrants and patents; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — consult the Pennsylvania State Archives for original land records.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County deed books from the colonial period onward
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783, just ended before this period); Quasi-War with France (1798–1800)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants. Pension files often include family depositions and are held at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives (archives.gov); Fold3 (fold3.com) has digitized Revolutionary War pension and service files

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, St. Peter's churchyard, and numerous denominational burial grounds; emergency/mass burials may have occurred during the 1793 epidemic
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) holds entries for Philadelphia-area burials
- **Physical records:** Church sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793 including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and the General Advertiser, which published lists of the dead during the epidemic
- **Where held:** American Antiquarian Society; Library of Congress; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) has some digitized holdings
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate sale notices, and Committee announcements published during the epidemic are primary genealogical sources; obituaries name surviving family members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry; the Port of Philadelphia received large numbers of immigrants from Germany, Ireland, Britain, and France throughout this period
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; naturalization records and declarations of intention (filed in Philadelphia courts, pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry.com has indexed Philadelphia-area passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania county tax lists; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax (a household-level enumeration covering real and personal property)
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County tax lists from the colonial period; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax covers the post-epidemic period
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; some holdings digitized on Ancestry.com
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census years and can document residence and property ownership for epidemic survivors

### Other record types
- **Yellow-fever-specific records:** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) lists names of the dead and is identified by the FamilySearch Wiki as a key genealogical source ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)); minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by citizens (Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania); Bush Hill hospital records (the main epidemic fever hospital, records at Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives)
- **City directories:** Philadelphia directories from 1785 onward list heads of household by name and address — valuable between census years and for documenting who returned to the city after the epidemic
- **Orphans' Court records:** Guardianship petitions for children orphaned by the epidemic (1793–1795) are held at the Philadelphia City Archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3,200,560 images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 federal censuses (indexed); Philadelphia passenger lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Philadelphia-area cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Selected historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | NARA finding aids and some digitized holdings | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for the Philadelphia/Pennsylvania area for this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800; 1 total result, complete result set). This is a significant digitization gap: most Philadelphia records from 1780–1810 are held on microfilm or physically rather than in searchable online collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Committee appointed by citizens records; Bush Hill hospital records; Orphans' Court records; city government records | In-person; finding aids online |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript collections relating to the epidemic; church records; city directories; newspapers; Bush Hill records | In-person; online catalog |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; some online via Ancestry partnership |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Pennsylvania Land Office records; state-level records; county tax lists | In-person; some online |
| Individual churches (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, etc.) | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each church directly |

## Records NOT online

- Philadelphia church baptism, marriage, and burial registers for most denominations: on FamilySearch microfilm but not name-indexed for 1793; some are physical-only at the churches or Historical Society of Pennsylvania
- Committee appointed by citizens manuscript minutes (Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania — physical only)
- Bush Hill hospital records (Historical Society of Pennsylvania — physical only)
- Philadelphia County deed books (physical at Recorder of Deeds; some microfilm at FamilySearch)
- Philadelphia County Orphans' Court records 1793–1800 (physical at Philadelphia City Archives)
- Philadelphia city directories 1785–1810 (some digitized in snippets; complete runs at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania)

## Known record losses

No major courthouse fire or flood is known to have destroyed Philadelphia County records for this period in the tool results consulted. The rapid pace of epidemic deaths in August–November 1793 means some individuals were buried without individual church registration. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies Mathew Carey's published account and the Committee's minutes as sources that partially compensate for gaps in church burial registers for this specific event. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

## Research tips

([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, Yellow Fever Epidemic 1793)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County formed 1682; city incorporated 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** City of Philadelphia (coextensive with the county for this period)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in 1793 (Wikipedia, Yellow fever epidemic of 1793). No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Major seaport and U.S. capital (1790–1800); trade, shipping, crafts, and finance dominated
- **Ethnic composition:** English, German, Irish, Scots-Irish, Dutch, African American; prominent Quaker community; sustained immigrant arrivals via the Port of Philadelphia
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers, Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Roman Catholic, Methodist
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 of ~50,000 residents (roughly one-tenth of the population); thousands fled the city. Philadelphia was the U.S. capital 1790–1800.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was formed in 1682 and remained geographically stable throughout the 1780–1810 period. The city and county were not formally consolidated until 1854. For this period, city and county records exist as distinct series but cover the same territory.
- No boundary changes affected the county during the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide vital registration until 1906 (state level). No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1793. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1793. Church registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the sole primary vital-record source for all events in this period.
- **Where held:** Individual denominational archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (which has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records)
- **Gaps:** Rapid epidemic deaths in August–November 1793 may have outpaced church registration capacity; some burials may be undocumented in any church register.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; Committee appointed by citizens records; Bush Hill hospital records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Quaker, Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Roman Catholic, Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; individual church archives; FamilySearch microfilm. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Yellow-fever-specific sources:** The FamilySearch Wiki specifically names burial records from Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as key sources for epidemic deaths. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))
- **Digitization:** 1 digitized volume on FamilySearch — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322), 145 images. Browse-only: 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Must be navigated image by image.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census (taken August 1790, three years before the epidemic) and the 1800 federal census are the two enumerations bracketing the event. Both are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania county tax lists serve as intercensal substitutes. The 1798 Federal Direct Tax enumerated every household, real property, and personal property in Philadelphia — a critical substitute record that falls between the 1790 and 1800 censuses.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed online (FamilySearch, Ancestry). The 1798 Federal Direct Tax is available on Ancestry.com.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, estate inventories, petitions; Orphans' Court guardianship cases (expected to have surged in 1793–1794 as epidemic orphans were placed)
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records from 1682 onward
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection ID 1999196) holds 3,200,560 images, browse-only (0 indexed records — must be navigated by date and ward). Also held at the Philadelphia Register of Wills and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Research priority:** Estate filings from late 1793 through 1795 document survivors, heirs, and family relationships for the approximately 5,000 epidemic dead — a high-priority source when vital records are absent.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is an original colony/state, not a federal public-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office issued warrants and patents; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — consult the Pennsylvania State Archives for original land records.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County deed books from the colonial period onward
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783, just ended before this period); Quasi-War with France (1798–1800)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants. Pension files often include family depositions and are held at NARA.
- **Where held:** National Archives (archives.gov); Fold3 (fold3.com) has digitized Revolutionary War pension and service files

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, St. Peter's churchyard, and numerous denominational burial grounds; emergency/mass burials may have occurred during the 1793 epidemic
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) holds entries for Philadelphia-area burials
- **Physical records:** Church sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793 including Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and the General Advertiser, which published lists of the dead during the epidemic
- **Where held:** American Antiquarian Society; Library of Congress; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) has some digitized holdings
- **Content value:** Death notices, estate sale notices, and Committee announcements published during the epidemic are primary genealogical sources; obituaries name surviving family members

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry; the Port of Philadelphia received large numbers of immigrants from Germany, Ireland, Britain, and France throughout this period
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; naturalization records and declarations of intention (filed in Philadelphia courts, pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record)
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Ancestry.com has indexed Philadelphia-area passenger lists
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania county tax lists; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax (a household-level enumeration covering real and personal property)
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County tax lists from the colonial period; the 1798 Federal Direct Tax covers the post-epidemic period
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; some holdings digitized on Ancestry.com
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the best substitute for missing census years and can document residence and property ownership for epidemic survivors

### Other record types
- **Yellow-fever-specific records:** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) lists names of the dead and is identified by the FamilySearch Wiki as a key genealogical source ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)); minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by citizens (Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania); Bush Hill hospital records (the main epidemic fever hospital, records at Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives)
- **City directories:** Philadelphia directories from 1785 onward list heads of household by name and address — valuable between census years and for documenting who returned to the city after the epidemic
- **Orphans' Court records:** Guardianship petitions for children orphaned by the epidemic (1793–1795) are held at the Philadelphia City Archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (3,200,560 images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312,045 indexed records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198,765 indexed records); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1790 and 1800 federal censuses (indexed); Philadelphia passenger lists; 1798 Federal Direct Tax | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Philadelphia-area cemetery inscriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Selected historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | NARA finding aids and some digitized holdings | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for the Philadelphia/Pennsylvania area for this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800; 1 total result, complete result set). This is a significant digitization gap: most Philadelphia records from 1780–1810 are held on microfilm or physically rather than in searchable online collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Committee appointed by citizens records; Bush Hill hospital records; Orphans' Court records; city government records | In-person; finding aids online |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Manuscript collections relating to the epidemic; church records; city directories; newspapers; Bush Hill records | In-person; online catalog |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; some online via Ancestry partnership |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Pennsylvania Land Office records; state-level records; county tax lists | In-person; some online |
| Individual churches (Christ Church, Gloria Dei, etc.) | Original baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact each church directly |

## Records NOT online

- Philadelphia church baptism, marriage, and burial registers for most denominations: on FamilySearch microfilm but not name-indexed for 1793; some are physical-only at the churches or Historical Society of Pennsylvania
- Committee appointed by citizens manuscript minutes (Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania — physical only)
- Bush Hill hospital records (Historical Society of Pennsylvania — physical only)
- Philadelphia County deed books (physical at Recorder of Deeds; some microfilm at FamilySearch)
- Philadelphia County Orphans' Court records 1793–1800 (physical at Philadelphia City Archives)
- Philadelphia city directories 1785–1810 (some digitized in snippets; complete runs at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania)

## Known record losses

No major courthouse fire or flood is known to have destroyed Philadelphia County records for this period in the tool results consulted. The rapid pace of epidemic deaths in August–November 1793 means some individuals were buried without individual church registration. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies Mathew Carey's published account and the Committee's minutes as sources that partially compensate for gaps in church burial registers for this specific event. ([FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

Here is the locality guide for Chicago and Cook County, Illinois during the Great Fire era:

---

## Chicago & Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire (1871) Locality Guide

**Coverage:** Cook County, Illinois, ca. 1860–1890, centered on the Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871.

---

### The Core Problem: Record Destruction

The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, taking with it nearly all:
- Pre-fire deeds
- Birth and death registers
- Probate files
- Court records
- Tax rolls

Pre-1871 vital events **cannot** be recovered from civil records at all.

---

### Surviving Post-Fire Collections (FamilySearch Indexed)

| Collection | Coverage | Est. Records |
|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 1871–1940 | ~1.45 million |
| Cook County Death Records | 1871–1947 | ~980,000 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1871–1920 | ~620,000 |
| Chicago Church Records | 1833–1925 | ~285,000 |

### Digitized Volumes (FamilySearch — browse/partial index)
- **Reconstructed Pre-Fire Court Records** (1865–1871) — 38 images, no name search
- **Burnt Record Act Property Re-Recordings** (1871–1880) — 112 images, ~41% name-indexed

---

### Substitute Sources for Pre-1871 Research

Because civil records were destroyed, use these alternatives:

1. **1870 Federal Census** — survived in Washington, D.C.; the best pre-fire population snapshot
2. **Chicago City Directories** — held at the **Newberry Library**; useful for locating families before the fire
3. **Church Registers** — the **Archdiocese of Chicago's Bernardin Archives** holds many pre-fire Catholic parish registers

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County formed 1831 from unorganized territory; Chicago incorporated as a city in 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** More than 100,000 residents were left homeless by the 1871 fire alone (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); population data from the FamilySearch tool returned empty for this survey
- **Economy:** Commercial and rail hub — meatpacking, lumber, and Great Lakes trade; rapid industrialization through the 1860s–1880s
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy immigration from Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia, and Bohemia; also a growing African American population
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (large Irish and German parishes), Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — killed approximately 300 people, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles, left 100,000+ homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse with most official records (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable through this period
- Illinois was a free state from admission in 1818; no significant jurisdictional split affects record location during 1860–1890

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has indexed collections of Cook County birth certificates (1871–1940, 1,450,000 records, collection 2024189), death records (1871–1947, 980,000 records, collection 1913456), and marriage records (1871–1920, 620,000 records, collection 1756321) — all beginning at the county level in 1871, the year of the fire
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (indexed + images) for post-fire records
- **Gaps:** Pre-fire birth, death, and marriage registers were destroyed when the Cook County Courthouse burned. The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey, so exact statewide registration start dates could not be confirmed; consult that page directly.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers (collection 1803978); city directories at the Newberry Library; the 1870 federal census

### Church records
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (285,000 records, collection 1803978), indexed — this is the primary source for pre-fire vital event data
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, and others; the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of Chicago archives (Catholic); denominational archives; FamilySearch microfilm; Newberry Library
- **Language:** German and Bohemian church records may require reading the original language

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860 and 1870 schedules for Chicago survived; the 1870 originals were held in Washington, D.C. and were not lost in the fire (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire); 1880 is also available; the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationwide
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses periodically; these may partially fill gaps around the fire year
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record persons who died in the year preceding each census
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianships, letters of administration, naturalization petitions
- **Gap:** Pre-fire probate files were held in the Cook County Courthouse and were destroyed in October 1871 (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **Post-fire:** Cook County probate records from 1871 onward are held at the Cook County Circuit Court Archives and the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Naturalizations:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record; many pre-fire filings were lost; post-fire records are at IRAD

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a public land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Land and Property page returned only generic content; the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office (BLM GLO) website holds federal land patents
- **Critical gap:** The courthouse fire destroyed original deed books and property records
- **Burnt Record Act:** The Illinois legislature passed the Burnt Record Act of 1872 requiring property owners to re-register their deeds; reconstructed deeds are a primary source for pre-fire property history (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Post-fire Property Re-recordings 1871–1880, imageGroupNumber 009982111, 112 images, 41% name-indexed — searchable by name on FamilySearch
- **Browse-only volume:** Pre-fire reconstructed court records 1865–1871, imageGroupNumber 009982110, 38 images, 0% name-indexed — must be browsed image by image with no search
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; IRAD at NEIU; Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); service and pension records were held federally and are not affected by the Chicago fire
- **Record types:** Union service records and pension files (NARA); draft registrations; Illinois state military records at the Illinois State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 (online, subscription); Illinois State Archives

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com covers major Chicago cemeteries including Graceland and Rosehill
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; some held at the Chicago History Museum

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (established 1847) and other Chicago papers; the Tribune survived the fire
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (online, subscription); Newberry Library (microfilm from the 1840s onward, source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, fire relief lists, legal notices (property re-registration notices), court notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New York (Castle Garden / later Ellis Island), Port of New Orleans, Port of Baltimore, and Great Lakes ports
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, declarations of intention, naturalization petitions, alien registrations
- **Where held:** NARA; Ancestry.com; FamilySearch (indexed passenger lists)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members. Many Cook County naturalization records were destroyed in 1871; check NARA for surviving federal court filings.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax and personal property tax
- **Gap:** Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed in the 1871 courthouse fire
- **Post-fire:** Cook County tax records from 1871 onward held at IRAD
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years — important given the near-total loss of 1890 federal census data nationwide

- **County and city histories:** 19th-century published histories of Cook County and Chicago often reprint early records that were later lost

| FamilySearch | Cook County Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000 records); Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000 records); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records (1865–1880) | Free |

Here is the locality guide for French colonial Louisiana:

---

**Locality Guide: Louisiana, French Colonial Period (1700s)**

You are researching ancestors in Louisiana during the 1700s, a period spanning both **French colonial rule (1699–1762)** and **Spanish colonial administration (effective 1769–1800)**. There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during this entire period.

---

### Primary Records: Catholic Church Parish Registers

The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized institution, and its parish registers — **baptisms, marriages, and burials** — are your primary source for vital family data.

**FamilySearch holdings:**
- **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** — roughly 987,000 indexed records; searchable by name
- **Sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803** — 264 images, browse-only (no name index)
- **French colonial notarial acts of the Superior Council, 1699–1769** — 149 images, browse-only

> ⚠️ The browse-only volumes are in **French and Spanish** and must be examined page by page.

---

### Notarial Records

**New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds notarial acts from the **1730s onward**, documenting family relationships through:
- Marriage contracts
- Estate inventories
- Property transactions

---

### Colonial Administrative Records

For census rolls, military rosters, and administrative correspondence, the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France is essential. It holds colonial-era material not available on FamilySearch.

---

### Key Research Warning: The French-to-Spanish Transition

The shift from French to Spanish rule in 1769 is a **temporal split, not a geographic one** — the same territory and parishes continued, but records shift from French to Spanish after that date. Search both series as a single continuous trail.

---

### Next Steps

1. Identify which **specific parish or parishes** your family was connected to.
2. Search the indexed **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** collection on FamilySearch first.
3. Then move to the **browse-only sacramental register volumes** and the **New Orleans Notarial Archives**.
4. For deeper colonial research, plan a query to **ANOM** in France.

For additional guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki at: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy)

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was claimed by France ca. 1682; the colony of Louisiane was formally established by 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 as the colonial capital, per the Wikipedia article on French Louisiana.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French Empire) 1699-1762; Spanish Empire (effective 1769-1800); briefly France again 1800-1803; United States from 1803
- **Population during period:** Population data for pre-statehood colonial Louisiana was not returned by the population tool.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture, fur trade, and river commerce; the Code Noir structured an enslaved labor economy.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, African enslaved people (required to be baptized Catholic under the Code Noir), Indigenous peoples, and some German and Swiss settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans 1718; France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain assumed effective administration 1769; retrocession to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812.

## Boundary changes
- **1699-1762:** French colonial Louisiana — an enormous territory from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico.
- **1762/1769:** France ceded the territory to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762); Spain assumed effective administrative control in 1769. This is a temporal split — records before 1769 are primarily in French, records from 1769 onward shift to Spanish. Both series are one continuous research trail for the same territory.
- **1800-1803:** Briefly retroceded to France, then sold to the United States (Louisiana Purchase). Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- The survey covers the full 1700s, spanning both the French (1700-1762) and Spanish colonial (1769-1800) eras.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the French or Spanish colonial period. There was no government-mandated registration of births, marriages, or deaths.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire colonial 1700s lacks civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers are the only vital record substitute — see Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons; no other denomination was legally recognized).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons), marriages, and burials. These are the single most important genealogical source for the colonial period.
- **Where held:**
  - St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) has registers from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
  - FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925** (id 1612905; 987,654 records): [familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — indexed, covering the colonial period.
  - FamilySearch also holds 1 browse-only digitized volume of sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720-1803 (264 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image; in French and Spanish).
- **Language:** French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). Researchers must read 18th-century French and Spanish or use a translator.

### Census records
- **Colonial census rolls:** No U.S. federal census covers the colonial period (U.S. census began 1790). The colonial administration conducted periodic censuses; these are held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Access:** ANOM online catalog at archives.culture.gouv.fr. Not on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, contracts, guardianships — generated by the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur), the colonial administrative and judicial body.
- **Date range:** 1699-1769 (French colonial); continued under Spanish colonial administration after 1769.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)). FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984** (id 2078341; 456,789 records): [familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341).
- FamilySearch also holds 1 browse-only digitized volume: French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699-1769 (149 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image; in French and Spanish).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish concession system — not the U.S. rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French colonial government issued concessions (grants); Spain continued the grant system. Documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and at the **Louisiana State Land Office**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, and notarial contracts (sales, mortgages, marriage settlements, powers of attorney).
- **Date range:** Notarial records available from the 1730s onward.
- **Where held:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) provides public access, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian conflicts; Seven Years' War period engagements.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia and troop lists (French colonial army lists).
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. No FamilySearch collection covering colonial Louisiana military records was returned by the tools.

### Cemetery records
- **Where held:** Burial records are part of the Catholic parish registers — the sacramental registers listed above. Separate sexton records are not expected for this period.
- **Online coverage:** Burial entries within **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925** (FamilySearch collection 1612905).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers in Louisiana appeared only in the late 18th century (Le Moniteur de la Louisiane began 1794, at the very end of the Spanish colonial period). No colonial-era newspaper archive was returned in tool results for the 1700-1793 window.
- **Where held:** Not a significant source for the pre-1790s period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary colonial port of entry).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and emigrant records for French colonial settlers are held at ANOM in Aix-en-Provence. No FamilySearch collection covering colonial immigration to Louisiana was returned by the tools.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property and poll taxes collected by colonial administrators.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans; and ANOM, France.
- **Substitute value:** Can confirm residency and approximate wealth when other records are absent.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — a major source for colonial family relationships, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (colonial sacramental registers and notarial acts) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-colonial); no Louisiana-specific colonial collection returned by tools | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records post-1803 | Free / in-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), France | Colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, military rosters, emigrant records | Online catalog; some digitized via Filae and Généanet |
| Fold3 | U.S. military records (post-1803) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana, 1700-1800 (totalResults: 2; both returned — this appears to be the complete set). Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records, colonial court and notarial records | In-person; partial digitization |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | In-person; some online |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | State and territorial records (post-1803) | In-person / online |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, military rosters | In-person; online catalog |
| St. Louis Cathedral Archives, New Orleans | Original parish registers from 1720 | Contact the Archdiocese of New Orleans |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-era census rolls (at ANOM, France) — not indexed or digitized on FamilySearch
- French colonial military and militia lists
- Pre-1730s notarial records (the notarial archive begins from the 1730s)
- Spanish-era administrative records (partially at Louisiana Historical Center, partially at ANOM)
- Colonial immigration and emigration passenger lists (at ANOM)

## Known record losses
- No specific destruction event was returned by the tools. The New Orleans area suffered repeated hurricane and fire damage throughout the colonial period. The Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM should be consulted directly for specific gap information.

## Research tips
- **Catholic church registers are the single most important source for the entire colonial period.** The Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons, so these registers may document enslaved people found in no other surviving record. See [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Two digitized volumes on FamilySearch are browse-only and in French/Spanish** — the sacramental registers (1720-1803, 264 images) and the Superior Council notarial acts (1699-1769, 149 images). Both must be browsed image by image with no name search. Researchers must be able to read 18th-century French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769).
- **Notarial acts are a powerful substitute for missing civil records.** Marriage contracts, estate settlements, property transactions, and powers of attorney name family members not otherwise documented. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access from the 1730s. See [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **For colonial census rolls, military records, and administrative correspondence,** the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France is an essential repository. Their catalog is at archives.culture.gouv.fr.
- **The French-to-Spanish transition is a temporal split (1762/1769), not a geographic one.** Records before 1769 are primarily in French; from 1769 they shift to Spanish. Both series cover the same territory and form one continuous research trail — research both together.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, Census, Naming Customs) all returned only generic content during this survey. Consult familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for the most current guidance.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was claimed by France ca. 1682; the colony of Louisiane was formally established by 1699. New Orleans was founded in 1718 as the colonial capital, per the Wikipedia article on French Louisiana.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French Empire) 1699-1762; Spanish Empire (effective 1769-1800); briefly France again 1800-1803; United States from 1803
- **Population during period:** Population data for pre-statehood colonial Louisiana was not returned by the population tool.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture, fur trade, and river commerce; the Code Noir structured an enslaved labor economy.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, African enslaved people (required to be baptized Catholic under the Code Noir), Indigenous peoples, and some German and Swiss settlers.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans 1718; France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain assumed effective administration 1769; retrocession to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana statehood 1812.

## Boundary changes
- **1699-1762:** French colonial Louisiana — an enormous territory from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico.
- **1762/1769:** France ceded the territory to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762); Spain assumed effective administrative control in 1769. This is a temporal split — records before 1769 are primarily in French, records from 1769 onward shift to Spanish. Both series are one continuous research trail for the same territory.
- **1800-1803:** Briefly retroceded to France, then sold to the United States (Louisiana Purchase). Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- The survey covers the full 1700s, spanning both the French (1700-1762) and Spanish colonial (1769-1800) eras.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the French or Spanish colonial period. There was no government-mandated registration of births, marriages, or deaths.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire colonial 1700s lacks civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers are the only vital record substitute — see Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively (the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons; no other denomination was legally recognized).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons), marriages, and burials. These are the single most important genealogical source for the colonial period.
- **Where held:**
  - St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) has registers from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
  - FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925** (id 1612905; 987,654 records): [familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — indexed, covering the colonial period.
  - FamilySearch also holds 1 browse-only digitized volume of sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720-1803 (264 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image; in French and Spanish).
- **Language:** French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). Researchers must read 18th-century French and Spanish or use a translator.

### Census records
- **Colonial census rolls:** No U.S. federal census covers the colonial period (U.S. census began 1790). The colonial administration conducted periodic censuses; these are held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Access:** ANOM online catalog at archives.culture.gouv.fr. Not on FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, contracts, guardianships — generated by the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur), the colonial administrative and judicial body.
- **Date range:** 1699-1769 (French colonial); continued under Spanish colonial administration after 1769.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)). FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984** (id 2078341; 456,789 records): [familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341).
- FamilySearch also holds 1 browse-only digitized volume: French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699-1769 (149 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image; in French and Spanish).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish concession system — not the U.S. rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French colonial government issued concessions (grants); Spain continued the grant system. Documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series and at the **Louisiana State Land Office**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, and notarial contracts (sales, mortgages, marriage settlements, powers of attorney).
- **Date range:** Notarial records available from the 1730s onward.
- **Where held:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) provides public access, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian conflicts; Seven Years' War period engagements.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia and troop lists (French colonial army lists).
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. No FamilySearch collection covering colonial Louisiana military records was returned by the tools.

### Cemetery records
- **Where held:** Burial records are part of the Catholic parish registers — the sacramental registers listed above. Separate sexton records are not expected for this period.
- **Online coverage:** Burial entries within **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925** (FamilySearch collection 1612905).

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Newspapers in Louisiana appeared only in the late 18th century (Le Moniteur de la Louisiane began 1794, at the very end of the Spanish colonial period). No colonial-era newspaper archive was returned in tool results for the 1700-1793 window.
- **Where held:** Not a significant source for the pre-1790s period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary colonial port of entry).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists and emigrant records for French colonial settlers are held at ANOM in Aix-en-Provence. No FamilySearch collection covering colonial immigration to Louisiana was returned by the tools.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property and poll taxes collected by colonial administrators.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans; and ANOM, France.
- **Substitute value:** Can confirm residency and approximate wealth when other records are absent.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — a major source for colonial family relationships, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 records); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (colonial sacramental registers and notarial acts) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-colonial); no Louisiana-specific colonial collection returned by tools | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records post-1803 | Free / in-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), France | Colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, military rosters, emigrant records | Online catalog; some digitized via Filae and Généanet |
| Fold3 | U.S. military records (post-1803) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana, 1700-1800 (totalResults: 2; both returned — this appears to be the complete set). Both are browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records, colonial court and notarial records | In-person; partial digitization |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | In-person; some online |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | State and territorial records (post-1803) | In-person / online |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, military rosters | In-person; online catalog |
| St. Louis Cathedral Archives, New Orleans | Original parish registers from 1720 | Contact the Archdiocese of New Orleans |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-era census rolls (at ANOM, France) — not indexed or digitized on FamilySearch
- French colonial military and militia lists
- Pre-1730s notarial records (the notarial archive begins from the 1730s)
- Spanish-era administrative records (partially at Louisiana Historical Center, partially at ANOM)
- Colonial immigration and emigration passenger lists (at ANOM)

## Known record losses
- No specific destruction event was returned by the tools. The New Orleans area suffered repeated hurricane and fire damage throughout the colonial period. The Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM should be consulted directly for specific gap information.

## Research tips
- **Catholic church registers are the single most important source for the entire colonial period.** The Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons, so these registers may document enslaved people found in no other surviving record. See [Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Two digitized volumes on FamilySearch are browse-only and in French/Spanish** — the sacramental registers (1720-1803, 264 images) and the Superior Council notarial acts (1699-1769, 149 images). Both must be browsed image by image with no name search. Researchers must be able to read 18th-century French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769).
- **Notarial acts are a powerful substitute for missing civil records.** Marriage contracts, estate settlements, property transactions, and powers of attorney name family members not otherwise documented. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access from the 1730s. See [Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **For colonial census rolls, military records, and administrative correspondence,** the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France is an essential repository. Their catalog is at archives.culture.gouv.fr.
- **The French-to-Spanish transition is a temporal split (1762/1769), not a geographic one.** Records before 1769 are primarily in French; from 1769 they shift to Spanish. Both series cover the same territory and form one continuous research trail — research both together.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Louisiana** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, Census, Naming Customs) all returned only generic content during this survey. Consult familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for the most current guidance.

Here is the locality guide from the research:

---

**Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Late 1800s Locality Guide**
*(Survey covers Schuylkill County, the anthracite coal heartland, 1870–1900)*

### Key Jurisdictional Facts

- **No Pennsylvania statewide vital registration** exists for this period. State death certificates only begin in **1906**. Births and marriages were not systematically registered either.
- This means **ethnic parish church registers** are effectively the only vital records for most mining families.

---

### Most Useful Record Types & Where to Find Them

| Record Type | Time Period | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Church registers** (Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, etc.) | Throughout the period | Individual parishes or denominational archives |
| **FamilySearch indexed marriage records** | 1870–1900 | FamilySearch.org |
| **Schuylkill County mine worker employment cards** | 1870–1900 | FamilySearch.org (digitized, name-searchable) — best single online starting point |
| **PA Mine Inspector annual reports** (fatal accident lists by name, age, nationality) | From 1870 | Pennsylvania State Library / Archives |
| **Naturalization records** | 1840s–1906 | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg |
| **Probate records** | Throughout the period | FamilySearch (digitized, unindexed — browse by image) |
| **Tax lists, city directories** | 1870–1900 | Local historical societies, county courthouses |
| **Federal censuses** (1870, 1880, 1900) | — | FamilySearch, Ancestry |

> ⚠️ **Note:** The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationwide. Tax lists, city directories, and church records are the best gap-fillers for that decade.

---

### Important Repositories

- **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) — naturalization records, state-level records
- **Individual ethnic parishes** — often the only source for births, marriages, and burials
- **FamilySearch.org** — mine employment cards, marriage records, probate images
- **County courthouses** — deeds, estates, some local civil records
- **Local/county historical societies** — city directories, newspapers, tax lists

---

### Geographic Scope Warning

Pennsylvania's coal region spans **multiple counties**: Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Columbia, and Northumberland, in addition to Schuylkill. Miners moved freely among them, so restricting a search to one county will likely miss family connections. Each county holds its own separate records.

---

**Recommended first step:** The **Schuylkill County mine worker employment cards (1870–1900)** on FamilySearch are the best online starting point for a coal-region ancestor. From there, identify the mining town and ethnic parish to locate church registers for vital events.

---

**Locality Guide: Massachusetts, 1620–1700 (Early Puritan Settlements)**

**Key Findings**

Massachusetts has some of the oldest civil records in North America. The Massachusetts Bay Colony required towns to register births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639**, and those town-level records survive in:

- A large **FamilySearch collection** (3.4+ million records)
- The published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series, covering more than 200 towns

**Congregational Church Records** are equally important — they predate the 1639 mandate and document baptisms, memberships, marriages, and disciplinary cases.

---

**Critical Jurisdictional Warning**

**Plymouth Colony (1620–1691)** and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** are two separate jurisdictions with separate record systems. If your family was in Plymouth before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records distinctly from Massachusetts Bay records.

---

**Population Substitutes (Pre-1790)**

No federal census exists before 1790. Key substitutes for this period include:
- **Freemen's lists**
- **Tax assessment rolls**
- **Church membership rolls**

---

**Most Useful Starting Point**

The **NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** at [americanancestors.org](https://americanancestors.org) identifies every known settler arriving between 1620 and 1643, with cited sources — this is the fastest path into documented early Massachusetts families.

---
