entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1629. These were **two distinct jurisdictions** throughout most of this period. Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **Administrative centers:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Massachusetts Bay Company
- **Population during period:** No population data available from tools for this era (federal census begins 1790). Wikipedia records approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration of 1630-1640.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and Atlantic trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; Indigenous Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and Narragansett peoples throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church of both colonies; small Quaker meetings and Baptist congregations appear from the 1650s-1680s
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640 (~20,000 English settlers); King Philip's War 1675-1676 (destroyed several frontier settlements and their records); Dominion of New England 1686-1689; Plymouth-Massachusetts merger 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1629-1692) were **separate jurisdictions** for almost the entire target period — records must be sought in each separately.
- After 1691, both colonies merge into the Province of Massachusetts Bay; Plymouth Colony records from 1620-1691 are published and indexed separately.
- Massachusetts Bay counties were established beginning 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); Plymouth County not created until 1685. Land and probate records organized at county level from those dates.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the Massachusetts Bay Colony in **1639** — at the **town level**, not county or colony level. This is among the earliest civil registration mandates in North America. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) — the primary indexed online source for this period.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colony-era originals. The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is available at NEHGS and many research libraries.
- **Gaps:** Plymouth Colony vital records are a separate series. No county-level or colony-wide vital registration existed; statewide civil registration began only in 1841.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are often the only record when the town entry is missing.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) is the established church and most thoroughly documented denomination. Small Quaker meetings and Baptist congregations appear by the 1650s-1680s.
- **Record types:** Membership admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments — these often name family relationships). Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records). FamilySearch volume 007612045 covers Congregational church admissions and baptisms in Suffolk County, 1630-1700 (121 images; **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — use keyword search). Published transcripts appear in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** First federal census is 1790 — **no federal census exists for the 1620-1700 period**.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No comprehensive territorial census survives. Town tax/rate lists and assessment rolls (Massachusetts Archives) serve as partial population substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Freemen's lists (admission to freeman status required church membership and was recorded from the 1630s) and church Half-Way Covenant membership rolls (from 1662) enumerate household heads; held at Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories of estate, and guardianships. Probate records begin in the 1630s at the county level.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records). County probate courts hold originals; Massachusetts Archives holds early colony-era records.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch wiki page for Massachusetts Probate Records returned only generic content during this survey — verify the page directly at familysearch.org/wiki.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey in this period)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land was granted by the General Court of Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony; individual towns also distributed land to town proprietors in successive "divisions." The specific wiki page for Massachusetts Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — verify directly.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, town proprietors' records, and mortgage documents. FamilySearch volume 007612044 holds town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698 (**188 images, browse-only, not name-indexed** — must be examined image by image).
- **Where held:** County Registries of Deeds hold deed books from the 1630s forward in remarkably complete runs. Massachusetts Archives holds colony-era grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1676) — the most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England; Pequot War (1636-1637).
- **Record types:** Colony muster rolls and expedition records, some published in the Massachusetts Archives documentary series. Pension and bounty land records post-date this period.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds most surviving militia records. Some muster rolls are published and available at NEHGS. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records but coverage for 1620-1700 is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Plymouth's Burial Hill (1620), Boston's King's Chapel Burying Ground (1630), Copp's Hill Burying Ground (1659), and numerous town burying grounds across both colonies.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Massachusetts colonial cemeteries with photographs of gravestones.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this early period; gravestone inscriptions and published cemetery transcriptions by local historical societies are the primary sources.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers circulated in Massachusetts during most of this period. "Publick Occurrences" (1690) was suppressed after one issue; "The Boston News-Letter" began in 1704, outside this window.
- **Substitute value:** Town meeting minutes, General Court records, and church disciplinary records substitute for news-era announcement content.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony).
- **Record types:** The FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" collection (ID 1784312) does **not** cover this period — it begins in 1820. Arrivals 1620-1700 are documented in published ship lists: John Camden Hotten's "Original Lists of Persons" (1600-1700); Charles Edward Banks's "Topographical Dictionary of 2885 English Emigrants" (1620-1650); James Savage's "Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New England."
- **Content note:** The "Great Migration" study series (NEHGS, Robert Charles Anderson) documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 with full source citations. Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony-era rate (tax assessment) lists and town "rates" survive for portions of this period.
- **Date range:** Fragmentary from the 1630s; more consistent from the 1650s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); some published in colonial records series.
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment lists confirm residency and can substitute for missing census-era enumerations.

### Other record types
- **General Court records:** Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records document land grants, freemen admissions, and judicial proceedings from the 1630s. Plymouth Colony equivalent records are published in "Plymouth Colony Records."
- **Freemen's lists:** Admissions to freeman status in Massachusetts Bay Colony required Congregational church membership and were recorded from the 1630s — these directly name household heads.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (3.4M records); Church Records 1630-1920 (987K records); Probate Records 1635-1991 (567K records) | Free |
| americanancestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | Membership/subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (limited for 1620-1700) | Subscription |
| archives.gov (NARA) | National Archives holdings (limited for colonial period) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period — both are detailed above; this is the complete set (totalResults: 2).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records from 1620s, court records, militia records, General Court records, tax/rate lists | In-person or written request |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | In-person (members); americanancestors.org (online) |
| County Registries of Deeds (counties est. 1643-1685) | Deed books from 1630s in complete runs | In-person; some digitized via county websites |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from 1630s | In-person; FamilySearch collection covers some |
| Pilgrim Hall Museum, Plymouth | Plymouth Colony records and published sources | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (FamilySearch volume 007612044, 188 images): scanned but **browse-only** — no name index, must be browsed image by image
- Colony militia/muster rolls (King Philip's War and Pequot War): primarily physical at Massachusetts Archives; some published in colonial records series
- Town tax/rate lists (1630s-1700): largely physical at Massachusetts Archives or in published compilations
- Pre-1700 church records outside Suffolk County: physical or microfilm only
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records: not in any online database; consult published ship lists (Hotten, Banks, Savage) in print or at NEHGS

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed frontier settlement records; towns including Deerfield, Brookfield, and Northfield were burned and their early records may not survive — consult published transcriptions for substitutes.
- No comprehensive colony-wide census was taken; population surveys for this period are fragmentary.
- Some early Plymouth Colony volumes are now known only through published transcriptions.

## Research tips
- **Start with the "Great Migration" series at NEHGS** (americanancestors.org): it documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 with full source citations, making it the single most efficient entry point for early Massachusetts families. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony are separate jurisdictions before 1691.** Search Plymouth Colony records (published in "Plymouth Colony Records") independently from Massachusetts Bay records.
- **Church records substitute for missing town vital records.** Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County 1630-1700 are full-text searchable in FamilySearch volume 007612045; outside Suffolk, check NEHGS and published Colonial Society transcripts. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Use the Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** — it abstracts town clerk records for over 200 towns and is the most efficient town-by-town search point for vital events in this period.
- **No federal census exists before 1790.** Use freemen's lists, church membership rolls, town tax/rate lists, and town proprietors' records as population substitutes.
- **Identify the specific town, not just the county.** Vital records, church records, and land divisions were recorded at the town level; a county-only search will miss town-specific series.

King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed records of several frontier towns including Deerfield and Brookfield — consider published transcriptions as substitutes.
FamilySearch volume 007612044 (town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698, 188 images) is browse-only with no name index — must be examined image by image.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1629. These were **two distinct jurisdictions** throughout most of this period. Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **Administrative centers:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Massachusetts Bay Company
- **Population during period:** No population data available from tools for this era (federal census begins 1790). Wikipedia records approximately 20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration of 1630-1640.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and Atlantic trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; Indigenous Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and Narragansett peoples throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church of both colonies; small Quaker meetings and Baptist congregations appear from the 1650s-1680s
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640 (~20,000 English settlers); King Philip's War 1675-1676 (destroyed several frontier settlements and their records); Dominion of New England 1686-1689; Plymouth-Massachusetts merger 1691

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1629-1692) were **separate jurisdictions** for almost the entire target period — records must be sought in each separately.
- After 1691, both colonies merge into the Province of Massachusetts Bay; Plymouth Colony records from 1620-1691 are published and indexed separately.
- Massachusetts Bay counties were established beginning 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk); Plymouth County not created until 1685. Land and probate records organized at county level from those dates.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the Massachusetts Bay Colony in **1639** — at the **town level**, not county or colony level. This is among the earliest civil registration mandates in North America. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) — the primary indexed online source for this period.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colony-era originals. The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is available at NEHGS and many research libraries.
- **Gaps:** Plymouth Colony vital records are a separate series. No county-level or colony-wide vital registration existed; statewide civil registration began only in 1841.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are often the only record when the town entry is missing.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) is the established church and most thoroughly documented denomination. Small Quaker meetings and Baptist congregations appear by the 1650s-1680s.
- **Record types:** Membership admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments — these often name family relationships). Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records). FamilySearch volume 007612045 covers Congregational church admissions and baptisms in Suffolk County, 1630-1700 (121 images; **full-text searchable but not name-indexed** — use keyword search). Published transcripts appear in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications.
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** First federal census is 1790 — **no federal census exists for the 1620-1700 period**.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No comprehensive territorial census survives. Town tax/rate lists and assessment rolls (Massachusetts Archives) serve as partial population substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Freemen's lists (admission to freeman status required church membership and was recorded from the 1630s) and church Half-Way Covenant membership rolls (from 1662) enumerate household heads; held at Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories of estate, and guardianships. Probate records begin in the 1630s at the county level.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records). County probate courts hold originals; Massachusetts Archives holds early colony-era records.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch wiki page for Massachusetts Probate Records returned only generic content during this survey — verify the page directly at familysearch.org/wiki.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (no rectangular survey in this period)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land was granted by the General Court of Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony; individual towns also distributed land to town proprietors in successive "divisions." The specific wiki page for Massachusetts Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — verify directly.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, town proprietors' records, and mortgage documents. FamilySearch volume 007612044 holds town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698 (**188 images, browse-only, not name-indexed** — must be examined image by image).
- **Where held:** County Registries of Deeds hold deed books from the 1630s forward in remarkably complete runs. Massachusetts Archives holds colony-era grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675-1676) — the most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England; Pequot War (1636-1637).
- **Record types:** Colony muster rolls and expedition records, some published in the Massachusetts Archives documentary series. Pension and bounty land records post-date this period.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds most surviving militia records. Some muster rolls are published and available at NEHGS. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds military records but coverage for 1620-1700 is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Plymouth's Burial Hill (1620), Boston's King's Chapel Burying Ground (1630), Copp's Hill Burying Ground (1659), and numerous town burying grounds across both colonies.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Massachusetts colonial cemeteries with photographs of gravestones.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this early period; gravestone inscriptions and published cemetery transcriptions by local historical societies are the primary sources.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers circulated in Massachusetts during most of this period. "Publick Occurrences" (1690) was suppressed after one issue; "The Boston News-Letter" began in 1704, outside this window.
- **Substitute value:** Town meeting minutes, General Court records, and church disciplinary records substitute for news-era announcement content.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony).
- **Record types:** The FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" collection (ID 1784312) does **not** cover this period — it begins in 1820. Arrivals 1620-1700 are documented in published ship lists: John Camden Hotten's "Original Lists of Persons" (1600-1700); Charles Edward Banks's "Topographical Dictionary of 2885 English Emigrants" (1620-1650); James Savage's "Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New England."
- **Content note:** The "Great Migration" study series (NEHGS, Robert Charles Anderson) documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 with full source citations. Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colony-era rate (tax assessment) lists and town "rates" survive for portions of this period.
- **Date range:** Fragmentary from the 1630s; more consistent from the 1650s onward.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); some published in colonial records series.
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment lists confirm residency and can substitute for missing census-era enumerations.

### Other record types
- **General Court records:** Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records document land grants, freemen admissions, and judicial proceedings from the 1630s. Plymouth Colony equivalent records are published in "Plymouth Colony Records."
- **Freemen's lists:** Admissions to freeman status in Massachusetts Bay Colony required Congregational church membership and were recorded from the 1630s — these directly name household heads.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890 (3.4M records); Church Records 1630-1920 (987K records); Probate Records 1635-1991 (567K records) | Free |
| americanancestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | Membership/subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (limited for 1620-1700) | Subscription |
| archives.gov (NARA) | National Archives holdings (limited for colonial period) | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume search returned 2 digitized volumes matching this place and period — both are detailed above; this is the complete set (totalResults: 2).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records from 1620s, court records, militia records, General Court records, tax/rate lists | In-person or written request |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies | In-person (members); americanancestors.org (online) |
| County Registries of Deeds (counties est. 1643-1685) | Deed books from 1630s in complete runs | In-person; some digitized via county websites |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from 1630s | In-person; FamilySearch collection covers some |
| Pilgrim Hall Museum, Plymouth | Plymouth Colony records and published sources | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (FamilySearch volume 007612044, 188 images): scanned but **browse-only** — no name index, must be browsed image by image
- Colony militia/muster rolls (King Philip's War and Pequot War): primarily physical at Massachusetts Archives; some published in colonial records series
- Town tax/rate lists (1630s-1700): largely physical at Massachusetts Archives or in published compilations
- Pre-1700 church records outside Suffolk County: physical or microfilm only
- Pre-1820 passenger arrival records: not in any online database; consult published ship lists (Hotten, Banks, Savage) in print or at NEHGS

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed frontier settlement records; towns including Deerfield, Brookfield, and Northfield were burned and their early records may not survive — consult published transcriptions for substitutes.
- No comprehensive colony-wide census was taken; population surveys for this period are fragmentary.
- Some early Plymouth Colony volumes are now known only through published transcriptions.

## Research tips
- **Start with the "Great Migration" series at NEHGS** (americanancestors.org): it documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 with full source citations, making it the single most efficient entry point for early Massachusetts families. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony are separate jurisdictions before 1691.** Search Plymouth Colony records (published in "Plymouth Colony Records") independently from Massachusetts Bay records.
- **Church records substitute for missing town vital records.** Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County 1630-1700 are full-text searchable in FamilySearch volume 007612045; outside Suffolk, check NEHGS and published Colonial Society transcripts. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Use the Tanner-Corbin "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** — it abstracts town clerk records for over 200 towns and is the most efficient town-by-town search point for vital events in this period.
- **No federal census exists before 1790.** Use freemen's lists, church membership rolls, town tax/rate lists, and town proprietors' records as population substitutes.
- **Identify the specific town, not just the county.** Vital records, church records, and land divisions were recorded at the town level; a county-only search will miss town-specific series.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Indian Territory (1889-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Unassigned Lands opened by the first Land Run on April 22, 1889. Oklahoma Territory formally established May 2, 1890 (Organic Act). Indian Territory existed alongside Oklahoma Territory under tribal and federal jurisdiction. Both merged at statehood on November 16, 1907.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Guthrie was the territorial capital; Oklahoma City became the state capital at statehood.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal government (Territory status); United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 settlers participated in the 1889 Land Run across roughly two million acres; the territory grew rapidly through subsequent land runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 (Wikipedia: Land Run of 1889).
- **Economy:** Agriculture (homesteading, wheat, cotton), cattle ranching; oil industry emerging in the early 1900s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers predominantly from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other southern/midwestern states; Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) in Indian Territory; freedmen (formerly enslaved persons of tribal members) documented in Dawes Commission records.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations established from 1889; Catholic missions predating the Run; FamilySearch holds mission and church records from 1820-1965.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run April 22, 1889; subsequent runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission tribal allotment 1898-1907; statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before May 2, 1890, the Unassigned Lands had no formal civil government.
- Oklahoma Territory expanded as successive land runs opened additional areas, reconfiguring county lines several times between 1890 and 1906.
- Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma) remained under separate tribal/federal jurisdiction until 1907.
- At statehood, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged. Records before 1907 may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" or "Indian Territory" depending on which side of the line the event occurred — search both.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; no Oklahoma-specific registration start year could be confirmed from tool results. No statewide civil registration of births and deaths existed during the territorial period (1890-1907); such registrations as existed were county-level.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2134789, 456,789 records, 913,578 persons). Birth and death registration for 1889-1907 is sparse with no territorial mandate.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for marriages; FamilySearch collection 2134789 is free online and searchable by name.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in the territorial period. Many early county records are incomplete.

- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations established from 1889; Catholic missions predating the Run; FamilySearch holds mission and church records from 1820-1965.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run April 22, 1889; subsequent runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission tribal allotment 1898-1907; statehood November 16, 1907.

## Boundary changes
- Before May 2, 1890, the Unassigned Lands had no formal civil government.
- Oklahoma Territory expanded as successive land runs opened additional areas, reconfiguring county lines several times between 1890 and 1906.
- Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma) remained under separate tribal/federal jurisdiction until 1907.
- At statehood, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged. Records before 1907 may be filed under "Oklahoma Territory" or "Indian Territory" depending on which side of the line the event occurred — search both.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; no Oklahoma-specific registration start year could be confirmed from tool results. No statewide civil registration of births and deaths existed during the territorial period (1890-1907); such registrations as existed were county-level.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2134789, 456,789 records, 913,578 persons). Birth and death registration for 1889-1907 is sparse with no territorial mandate.
- **Where held:** County courthouses for marriages; FamilySearch collection 2134789 is free online and searchable by name.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in the territorial period. Many early county records are incomplete.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; homestead final proof affidavits naming family members; Indian census records; territorial court records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic (missions pre-1889), and other Protestant denominations from 1889.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations; mission records from 1820.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 ("Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965"), 123,456 records with images — indexed + images. Denominational archives hold additional undigitized material.
- **Language:** English; some early Catholic mission records may be in Latin or Spanish.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire in 1921. The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are fully available and indexed. There is no 1880 federal census for Oklahoma (the territory did not exist).
- **1890 territorial special census:** Oklahoma Territory had a special territorial census taken in 1890, one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation, held by the Oklahoma Historical Society (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **1907 statehood census:** Oklahoma conducted a special census at statehood — a unique resource documenting residents at the moment of statehood. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Indian censuses:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 ("Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959"), 567,890 indexed records with images — indexed + images.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are online and indexed (FamilySearch, Ancestry). Indian censuses are online free at FamilySearch. The 1890 territorial census and 1907 statehood census are physical-only at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, naturalization petitions, civil and criminal suits.
- **Date range:** From territorial organization (1890) through statehood (1907) and beyond.
- **Where held:** Territorial district court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Post-statehood county probate is at county courthouses.
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record including territorial district courts — NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives are the primary repositories.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (Public Land Survey System), administered by the General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (General Land Office); initial homestead applications and patents filed at land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher (Wikipedia: Land Run of 1889).
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final proof certificates, land patents; also town lot records and subsequent deeds at county level.
- **Date range:** From April 22, 1889.
- **Where held:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1541872 ("Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907"): 234,567 records, 117,283 images — indexed + images.
  - FamilySearch volume 005221388 (land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889-1907): 402 images, 74% name-indexed — indexed + images.
  - NARA Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office): original homestead files; rejected applications also survive with family details (per FamilySearch Wiki).
  - BLM General Land Office Records (glorecords.blm.gov): partially indexed patents, free online (per FamilySearch Wiki).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898); Civil War pension payments to surviving veterans and widows continued throughout this period.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA; pension files especially relevant for Land Run settlers who were Civil War veterans.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.); Fold3 online for some military records; state adjutant general records at Oklahoma State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Established alongside new towns from 1889; many associated with churches or townships.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has Oklahoma cemetery transcriptions; coverage varies by county and era.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers from 1889; many early burials were in family or community plots without formal records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Territorial newspapers began in new towns from 1889 (Guthrie, Oklahoma City, Kingfisher, and others).
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com for digitized historical Oklahoma newspapers; Oklahoma Historical Society holds microfilm; Library of Congress Chronicling America project.
- **Content value:** Homestead legal notices, land claim disputes, marriage announcements, obituaries, coverage of Sooner/Boomer controversy.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant context:** Most Land Run settlers migrated internally from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. For foreign-born settlers, naturalization was filed in territorial district courts before 1906.
- **Record types:** Naturalization records in territorial courts (NARA Fort Worth); passenger lists at NARA for any immigrant settlers.
- **Where held:** NARA for passenger lists; NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives for pre-1906 naturalizations.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard including infants and young children. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property schedules from the 1890s.
- **Date range:** From territorial county organization (1890).
- **Where held:** County courthouses and Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** County tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers between census years and partially substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census (per FamilySearch Wiki).

### Other record types
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (1898-1910):** FamilySearch volume 005221389, 176 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only images. These are the application files for tribal citizenship enrollment among the Five Civilized Tribes, containing family details, affidavits, and testimony. Anyone with Native American, freedmen, or intermarried-white ancestry in Indian Territory must browse these image by image with no search capability.
- **Indian Territory records:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 covers Indian censuses and rolls 1851-1959 with 567,890 indexed records. Separate from Oklahoma Territory records.
- **Town lot records:** Many Land Run participants claimed town lots rather than rural homesteads; these are at county courthouses and partially in GLO files.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834-1907 (234,567 records); Indian Censuses and Rolls 1851-1959 (567,890 records); County Marriages 1890-1995 (456,789 records); Mission and Church Records 1820-1965 (123,456 records); land-entry case files 1889-1907 (74% indexed); Dawes enrollment jackets 1898-1910 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents, partially indexed | Free |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Homestead files (RG 49), territorial court records, naturalization | Some free; in-person or mail order |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for this place and period; both are the complete result set (totalResults: 2).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory court records 1890-1907, pre-1906 naturalization records | In-person / NARA research request |
| NARA Washington, D.C. | General Land Office homestead files (RG 49), military records | In-person / mail order |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 territorial special census, 1907 statehood census, territorial newspapers | In-person / some online |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial court records, county records, state vital records post-1907 | In-person / mail |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate records, marriage records, tax rolls | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census (Oklahoma Historical Society) — not fully digitized
- The 1907 Oklahoma statehood census — contact Oklahoma Historical Society
- Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (volume 005221389): images exist online but are browse-only with no name index
- Most county-level tax records from the 1890s
- Many early church records not in the FamilySearch mission/church collection
- Original homestead case files at NARA RG 49 (some indexed via FamilySearch and BLM GLO; full case file requires NARA request)

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire in Washington, D.C. in 1921. Substitute sources: 1890 Oklahoma territorial special census (Oklahoma Historical Society), county tax rolls, GLO land records, and the 1900 federal census.
- Some early county courthouse records were lost during the rapid territorial organization period of the 1890s.

## Research tips
- **Start with the land.** The homestead file is the central document for any Land Run family — it names the claimant, lists family members as witnesses, and proves presence on the specific quarter-section. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and the BLM GLO records site (glorecords.blm.gov) first (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Trace origins before Oklahoma.** Once you find the settler in Oklahoma, search departure-state records (birth, marriage, earlier census) in Kansas, Texas, Missouri, or wherever they came from (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts).
- **Search both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.** If ancestry could include Native American, freedmen, or intermarried-white in Indian Territory, also search the Dawes Commission rolls (FamilySearch volume 005221389, browse-only) and Indian census collection 1987432.
- **The 1890 census gap is partially filled.** Oklahoma is one of the rare jurisdictions with a surviving 1890 special territorial census — contact the Oklahoma Historical Society for access.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial courts.** Foreign-born Land Run settlers who naturalized before 1906 filed in any territorial court of record — NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives hold these files.
- **Rejected homestead applications survive.** A claimant who lost a land contest still generated a file at NARA RG 49 that may contain family details (per FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).

Here is the locality guide produced for **Alabama circa 1800**:

---

## Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (~1800) — Locality Research Guide

### Critical Jurisdictional Context
The Alabama region around 1800 was **not yet a state**. It was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (organized 1798), and the Mobile area had previously been under **French, then British, then Spanish** colonial rule. This means:

- Most surviving records from this period are filed under *Mississippi*, not Alabama.
- Spanish and French colonial records exist for Mobile and the Gulf Coast area, some held in archives in France and Spain, with copies at the Library of Congress.

---

### Key Record Types & Where to Find Them

**FamilySearch (indexed, searchable by name):**
Eight name-indexed collections cover this period and territory, including:
- **Land records** (back to ~1792 under Mississippi jurisdiction)
- **Court records**
- **Church records**
- **Census substitutes**
- **Marriage records**
- **Early Alabama records (from ~1803)**
- **Probate records**

**Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery:**
This is the essential repository for undigitized territorial-era material, including:
- **Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**
- **Militia rolls**
- **Early county records**

---

### Digitized/Browsable (Unindexed) Volumes
> ⚠️ **No digitized, browsable image volumes were found in FamilySearch's catalog for the pre-statehood Alabama/Mississippi Territory period.** The coverage gap is real. Browsable unindexed records must currently be sought at ADAH directly.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Search the eight FamilySearch indexed collections** by name for specific ancestors.
2. **Contact ADAH** for territorial-era material not yet digitized.
3. If your ancestor was in the **Mobile area**, expect records in **French or Spanish** — look to the Library of Congress and European archives for copies.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory), ca. 1790–1820

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Alabama became a state December 14, 1819. The present-day territory was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then the Alabama Territory from 1817 to 1819. Before 1798 the interior was part of Georgia's western land claim; the Mobile area was French colonial territory (1702–1763), then British (1763–1780), then Spanish (1780–1813).
- **County seat / administrative center:** The territorial capital was Natchez (in present-day Mississippi) through most of the period; Huntsville served the Alabama Territory from 1817; Cahaba briefly became Alabama state capital after 1820.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819), then U.S. statehood (1819).
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the population tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Agriculture (cotton, tobacco), fur trade, and subsistence farming; the interior was largely unsettled by Europeans until after the Creek War of 1813–1814.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations held most of the interior; European-American settlers concentrated in the Tennessee Valley (north) and Tombigbee River valley; French and Spanish Creoles and enslaved Africans in the Mobile area; significant enslaved African-American population throughout.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes in Mobile (continuous since the French period); Methodist circuit riders; Baptist missionaries; Presbyterian missions to Native nations.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War of 1813–1814 opened the interior to rapid Euro-American settlement; Fort Mims massacre (1813); Treaty of Fort Jackson (1814) transferred Creek lands.

## Boundary changes

- **Before 1798:** Present-day Alabama was claimed by Georgia (interior) and Spain (Mobile area). No U.S. territorial government existed over this territory.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory established; initially covered only the southern strip of present-day Mississippi and Alabama.
- **1804:** Eastern portion (roughly present-day Alabama, excluding the Mobile area) added to Mississippi Territory.
- **1810–1813:** Mobile District (held by Spain) taken over by the United States in 1813.
- **1817:** Eastern Mississippi Territory separated as the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted to the Union as the 22nd state.

**Critical research implication:** Records created in present-day Alabama before 1817 were generated under the Mississippi Territory jurisdiction and are typically filed as *Mississippi* records — not Alabama. Searching Alabama alone will miss the bulk of the pre-statehood series. Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860–1890)

### Geographic Overview

The anthracite coal region spans five core counties:

- **Schuylkill** – the historical heart of the region
- **Luzerne** – note that **Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878**; all pre-1878 Lackawanna-area events must be searched in Luzerne County records
- **Lackawanna** (formed 1878 from Luzerne)
- **Carbon**
- **Northumberland**

Schuylkill County's population grew from ~89,500 (1860) to nearly 130,000 (1880), driven almost entirely by Irish and Eastern European immigrant miners.

---

### Catholic Church / Diocese Jurisdiction — Critical Complication

The **Diocese of Scranton was created in 1868**. This splits Irish Catholic parish records:

| County | Before 1868 | After 1868 |
|---|---|---|
| Luzerne / Lackawanna | Diocese of Philadelphia | **Diocese of Scranton** |
| Northumberland | Diocese of Philadelphia | Diocese of Harrisburg |
| Schuylkill / Carbon | Diocese of Philadelphia | Diocese of Philadelphia (unchanged) |

Always check the correct diocesan archives for the right period.

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Records (Schuylkill County)

Five volume sets are digitized on FamilySearch for 1849–1915:

| Record Type | Dates | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Naturalization records | 1849–1915 | Browse only (no name index) |
| Probate records | 1851–1930 | Browse only |
| Church records (English & German) | 1842–1895 | Browse only |
| Deed records | 1815–1900 | ~22% indexed |
| Marriage records | 1870–1910 | Browse only |

**Most volumes require page-by-page browsing** — no name index, no full-text search.

---

### Specialized Coal-Region Indexes (High Priority)

The FamilySearch wiki page for **Pennsylvania Coal Region Records** documents two specialized finding aids:

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** – names ~41,000 colliery workers with occupation and **parish of origin** (invaluable for tracing Irish immigrants back to their home parishes)
2. **Pennsylvania Triennial Tax Assessments (from 1853)** – record occupation and sometimes nativity, filling in gaps between census years

These are high-priority sources for Irish miners between census years.

---

### Research Strategy Notes

- Each of the five coal counties needs its own locality survey
- For Lackawanna-area events **before 1878**, search Luzerne County records
- The `research-plan` skill can build a step-by-step search sequence from this guide
- Consider the FamilySearch wiki page at:
  `https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records`

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Schuylkill County (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (source: place_search_all)
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860 US Census), 116,428 (1870), 129,974 (1880) — source: place_population tool
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery employment (loading, breaking, hauling) dominated the regional workforce throughout the period
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population; Eastern European immigrants arriving later in the period; German-speaking communities present (church records appear in English and German)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Lutheran; German Reformed; Methodist; other Protestant denominations
- **Key historical events:** Civil War draft and military service (1861-1865); Molly Maguires labor conflict and trials (1875-1877); rapid colliery expansion and population growth across the full period

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout the 1860-1890 period.
- In the broader anthracite region: **Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878.** All records for events in the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre area before 1878 were created and filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne County first for any pre-1878 events, then Lackawanna for 1878 onward.
- Schuylkill County itself was formed in 1811; records predating formation would be under Berks or Northampton counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and did not state a specific civil registration start year or level. The page for confirmed dates is https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records.
- **What exists:** 1 digitized volume of Marriage Records, 1870-1910 (94 images, imageGroup 007936753, **browse-only**, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (Pottsville); FamilySearch digital images (browse-only)
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth or death record volumes for 1860-1890 were returned by volume_search. Civil registration for births and deaths was likely absent or irregular in Pennsylvania during this period at the statewide level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; mortality schedules in the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses; coroner's inquest records for mine accident deaths

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrants, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records); Lutheran; German Reformed; other Protestant
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** 1 digitized volume of Church Records, 1842-1895 (187 images, imageGroup 007936751, **browse-only**, 0% indexed, English and German). Diocese of Philadelphia held all five anthracite counties before 1868; from 1868 Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton, Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was established in 1961. For Schuylkill County Catholic registers throughout the 1860-1890 period, contact the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives.
- **Language:** English and German; sacramental entries may appear in Latin
- **Note:** The collections_search tool also returned a record labeled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) — this is flagged in the tool output as a synthetic test fixture and should not be treated as a genuine archival collection.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations cover Schuylkill County; the 1890 federal census was **destroyed nationally** — it does not exist for any county
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no intercensal state census in this period
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each enumeration — an important substitute for absent civil death registration; available on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Access:** Federal censuses are name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; external_links_search returned an Ancestry link for the 1850 Schuylkill County census, and the 1860-1880 enumerations are accessible through Ancestry's nationwide indexed collections

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Digitized volume covers 1851-1930; broader collection (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994, collection 1999196) covers to 1994
- **Where held:** 1 digitized volume of Probate Records, 1851-1930 (412 images, imageGroup 007936749, **browse-only**, 0% indexed); Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images, **browse-only**, 0 indexed records). Physical originals at Schuylkill County courthouse.
- **Note:** Irish coal-miner families often died without wills (intestate) — search administrations and guardianship files, not just the will books. The Molly Maguires trials (Schuylkill County Court of Quarter Sessions, 1875-1877) generated court records naming many Irish-born defendants and witnesses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land, not federal public-land, state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; the specific granting authority and records office are not confirmed from a tool result in this run
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; 1 digitized volume of Deed Records, 1815-1900 (543 images, imageGroup 007936752, **22% name-indexed** — the only partially-indexed volume in the Schuylkill County digitized set)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch partially-indexed images online
- **Note:** Wage-earning miners rarely owned land, so deed records are most useful for landlords, mine operators, and boarding-house keepers

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Civil War service records; pension files; 1863 and 1864 draft registration records (particularly valuable for Irish immigrant miners who were subject to the draft); bounty land warrants; state adjutant general compiled service records
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry); draft records at NARA RG 110; Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records; FamilySearch has some Civil War record collections

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries associated with coal-region parishes; non-denominational and Protestant community cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide online coverage; external_links_search did not return a specific FindAGrave or BillionGraves Schuylkill County collection for this period
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemetery organizations or parishes; some transcribed by the Schuylkill County Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) is the most significant paper for the coal region and covered the 1860-1890 period; it documented the Molly Maguires trials extensively, naming Irish-born defendants and family members
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, coroner's inquest reports on mine accidents, labor news, and legal notices
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library; Schuylkill County Historical Society; Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for any digitized runs; check local libraries for microfilm

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York/Castle Garden (pre-Ellis Island); Irish immigrants of the 1840s-1860s typically arrived through these ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (1 digitized volume of Naturalization Records, 1849-1915, 298 images, imageGroup 007936750, **browse-only**, 0% indexed); affidavits filed by relatives; alien registrations
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Court naturalization volume on FamilySearch (browse-only); NARA Philadelphia for federal court naturalization records; Ancestry for indexed passenger lists; FamilySearch Castle Garden/NARA records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Naturalization declarations (first papers) and petitions (second papers) filed before 1906 could be lodged in any court of record — browse the county volume and check NARA federal courts.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (coal-region residents enumerated every three years from 1853); real estate assessment; personal property tax
- **Date range:** 1853 onward; assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county assessor records
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments fill the 1861, 1864, 1867, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1880, 1883, 1886, 1889 intercensal gaps; occupation listings can confirm a person worked in the coal industry; nativity notations can confirm Irish origin. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records

### Specialized coal-region records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. Use this as a specialized finding aid before or alongside census searches. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Mine inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery rather than by person — useful for establishing where a miner worked but not for name searches; held at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Coal company payroll books:** The source from which the Anthracite Index was derived; originals (where they survive) are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, Delaware

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1860-1890) was the heart of the anthracite coal region, with population growing from about 89,500 in 1860 to nearly 130,000 by 1880, driven almost entirely by Irish and Eastern European immigrant miners working the collieries. Five digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch for this county in the period: naturalization records (1849-1915), probate records (1851-1930), church records (1842-1895 in English and German), deed records (1815-1900, partially indexed at 22%), and marriage records (1870-1910). All but the deed records must be browsed image by image with no name index and no full-text search. A specialized wiki page for the Pennsylvania coal region (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) describes the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index naming roughly 41,000 colliery workers with occupation and parish of origin, and Pennsylvania's triennial tax assessments from 1853 that record occupation and sometimes nativity — both are high-priority sources between census years. For Irish Catholic ancestry, the critical complication is the diocese split of 1868: before that date all five coal counties' Catholic parish records fall under the Diocese of Philadelphia; from 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna moved to the Diocese of Scranton, Northumberland to Harrisburg, while Schuylkill and Carbon stayed with Philadelphia. The neighboring coal counties of Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland each need their own locality survey, and any Lackawanna-area event before 1878 must be searched in Luzerne County records, since Lackawanna did not exist as an independent county until that year.

Research planning with the `research-plan` skill can now build a step-by-step search sequence using this locality guide.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Schuylkill County (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties (source: place_search_all)
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860 US Census), 116,428 (1870), 129,974 (1880) — source: place_population tool
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; colliery employment (loading, breaking, hauling) dominated the regional workforce throughout the period
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish immigrant population; Eastern European immigrants arriving later in the period; German-speaking communities present (church records appear in English and German)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Lutheran; German Reformed; Methodist; other Protestant denominations
- **Key historical events:** Civil War draft and military service (1861-1865); Molly Maguires labor conflict and trials (1875-1877); rapid colliery expansion and population growth across the full period

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout the 1860-1890 period.
- In the broader anthracite region: **Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878.** All records for events in the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre area before 1878 were created and filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne County first for any pre-1878 events, then Lackawanna for 1878 onward.
- Schuylkill County itself was formed in 1811; records predating formation would be under Berks or Northampton counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey and did not state a specific civil registration start year or level. The page for confirmed dates is https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records.
- **What exists:** 1 digitized volume of Marriage Records, 1870-1910 (94 images, imageGroup 007936753, **browse-only**, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse (Pottsville); FamilySearch digital images (browse-only)
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth or death record volumes for 1860-1890 were returned by volume_search. Civil registration for births and deaths was likely absent or irregular in Pennsylvania during this period at the statewide level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial registers; mortality schedules in the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses; coroner's inquest records for mine accident deaths

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (established 1840-1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrants, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records); Lutheran; German Reformed; other Protestant
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** 1 digitized volume of Church Records, 1842-1895 (187 images, imageGroup 007936751, **browse-only**, 0% indexed, English and German). Diocese of Philadelphia held all five anthracite counties before 1868; from 1868 Luzerne and Lackawanna transferred to the Diocese of Scranton, Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained under Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was established in 1961. For Schuylkill County Catholic registers throughout the 1860-1890 period, contact the Diocese of Philadelphia Archives.
- **Language:** English and German; sacramental entries may appear in Latin
- **Note:** The collections_search tool also returned a record labeled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) — this is flagged in the tool output as a synthetic test fixture and should not be treated as a genuine archival collection.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 enumerations cover Schuylkill County; the 1890 federal census was **destroyed nationally** — it does not exist for any county
- **State census:** Pennsylvania conducted no intercensal state census in this period
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each enumeration — an important substitute for absent civil death registration; available on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Access:** Federal censuses are name-indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; external_links_search returned an Ancestry link for the 1850 Schuylkill County census, and the 1860-1880 enumerations are accessible through Ancestry's nationwide indexed collections

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Digitized volume covers 1851-1930; broader collection (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994, collection 1999196) covers to 1994
- **Where held:** 1 digitized volume of Probate Records, 1851-1930 (412 images, imageGroup 007936749, **browse-only**, 0% indexed); Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images, **browse-only**, 0 indexed records). Physical originals at Schuylkill County courthouse.
- **Note:** Irish coal-miner families often died without wills (intestate) — search administrations and guardianship files, not just the will books. The Molly Maguires trials (Schuylkill County Court of Quarter Sessions, 1875-1877) generated court records naming many Irish-born defendants and witnesses.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land, not federal public-land, state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; the specific granting authority and records office are not confirmed from a tool result in this run
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages; 1 digitized volume of Deed Records, 1815-1900 (543 images, imageGroup 007936752, **22% name-indexed** — the only partially-indexed volume in the Schuylkill County digitized set)
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch partially-indexed images online
- **Note:** Wage-earning miners rarely owned land, so deed records are most useful for landlords, mine operators, and boarding-house keepers

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Civil War service records; pension files; 1863 and 1864 draft registration records (particularly valuable for Irish immigrant miners who were subject to the draft); bounty land warrants; state adjutant general compiled service records
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry); draft records at NARA RG 110; Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records; FamilySearch has some Civil War record collections

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries associated with coal-region parishes; non-denominational and Protestant community cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide online coverage; external_links_search did not return a specific FindAGrave or BillionGraves Schuylkill County collection for this period
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemetery organizations or parishes; some transcribed by the Schuylkill County Historical Society

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville) is the most significant paper for the coal region and covered the 1860-1890 period; it documented the Molly Maguires trials extensively, naming Irish-born defendants and family members
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, coroner's inquest reports on mine accidents, labor news, and legal notices
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library; Schuylkill County Historical Society; Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for any digitized runs; check local libraries for microfilm

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York/Castle Garden (pre-Ellis Island); Irish immigrants of the 1840s-1860s typically arrived through these ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists; declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (1 digitized volume of Naturalization Records, 1849-1915, 298 images, imageGroup 007936750, **browse-only**, 0% indexed); affidavits filed by relatives; alien registrations
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Court naturalization volume on FamilySearch (browse-only); NARA Philadelphia for federal court naturalization records; Ancestry for indexed passenger lists; FamilySearch Castle Garden/NARA records
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. Naturalization declarations (first papers) and petitions (second papers) filed before 1906 could be lodged in any court of record — browse the county volume and check NARA federal courts.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (coal-region residents enumerated every three years from 1853); real estate assessment; personal property tax
- **Date range:** 1853 onward; assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county assessor records
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments fill the 1861, 1864, 1867, 1871, 1874, 1877, 1880, 1883, 1886, 1889 intercensal gaps; occupation listings can confirm a person worked in the coal industry; nativity notations can confirm Irish origin. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records

### Specialized coal-region records
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855-1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. Use this as a specialized finding aid before or alongside census searches. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Mine inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery rather than by person — useful for establishing where a miner worked but not for name searches; held at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Coal company payroll books:** The source from which the Anthracite Index was derived; originals (where they survive) are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, Delaware

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide

Vermont is one of the most distinctive pre-statehood research challenges in American genealogy. The territory you are researching did not exist as a formal state jurisdiction until March 4, 1791, meaning your ancestors lived first under the contested **New Hampshire Grants**, then under the **Republic of Vermont (1777–1791)**.

### Key Finding Aid
The single most important resource the FamilySearch wiki documents for this era is the **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**, which enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire land grants that New York refused to recognize — the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.

### Civil Registration
Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths did **not begin until 1857**, so for your pre-statehood period there is no civil registration at all. Town clerk vital records survive unevenly from the 1770s. The primary sources for vital events are:
- Church registers
- Probate files
- Tax lists
- Town proprietary records

### Census Coverage
The **1790 federal census** (the first year Vermont was enumerated) names only heads of household.

### Jurisdictional Complexity
For pre-1777 events, records may be held in:
- **New Hampshire State Archives** — Benning Wentworth grant files
- **New York State Archives** — competing patents

This is not a clean before-and-after split; it depends on which colonial authority each settler dealt with.

### Research Caveat
The FamilySearch Catalog could not be fully enumerated in this survey. Run a direct search at [familysearch.org/search/catalog](https://familysearch.org/search/catalog) before treating any absence as confirmed.
